maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.

speechtext:
House in Committee on Bill (No. 150) respecting the Restigouche Boom Company, and to change its name to the Restigouche Log Driving and Boom Company.-Mr. Reid (Restigouche).
On section 2,

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: Has this Bill been reported favourably by the Private Bills Committee?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: The copy I have says it is reported as amended by the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: Yes. There were representatives at the committee of the Boom Company, the riparian owners, the anglers and the fishermen. There was one change made at the request of some of the members of the committee, but all the others were made at the request of the interested parties, and when the Bill left the committee there was a thorough understanding among all the parties concerned. I may state that after consulting with Mr. Speaker, in whose county these works will be located, I propose to make two very slight amendments. One is to provide that there shall be no question that the man who rafts his logs will have the right to run them down the river without interference, and will not have to pay any charges, and the section 26 dealing with the expropriation of lands and rights. With these two slight amendments the Bill is now perfectly satisfactory to all parties concerned who are represented, and I think that all parties imaginable were represented before the committee either in person or by counsel.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: I would like to ask on what ground the committee reported that this was a work for the general advantage of Canada?

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not think those words were necessary, because the works are on both sides of an interprovincial river. But it was thought best by the committee to insert those words to avoid any question of jurisdiction. I may explain that for a great many years the lumber has been driven down the Restigouche river and has been boomed and rafted on the New Brunswick side. Ten years ago fifteen or twenty million feet of lumber came down the river. This year there will be at least 125,000,000 feet, and the booms are wholly inadequate to take care of that enormous quantity of lumber. Last year a large quantity went out to sea and some of it was lost. It is proposed to have all the lumber rafted down and boomed by the same company both on the Quebec side and on the New Brunswick side, so that I submit that this parliament alone will have jurisdiction without the insertion of those words.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: I am not finding any fault with the project. I dare .say if may be a very useful one, as I understand that a combination is proposed of the various interests concerned in driving logs on this river for the purpose of doing the work more effectively than it has been done in the past. It is a perfectly legitimate proposition provided the rights of the public are preserved; but I do not think that the declaration that this is an undertaking for the general advantage of Canada ought to be lightly made. I have been of the opinion that on a good many occasions it has been too lightly made by this parliament. If it is not essential in this case, I would think it far better to omit it.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext:
While the incorporators might possibly get all they are with-

out these words in the Bill, yet certain works must be performed wholly within the province of New Brunswick and others wholly in the province of Quebec. I have discussed the question with the solicitor of the company, and it is at his request that the words are left in the Bill.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works, who has paid some attention to this Bill, what he understands to be the meaning of these words in this section, ' nothing herein contained shall affect any action heretofore taken pursuant to the powers in such act contained.' Is that intended to refer to a legal action or an ordinary action?

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: I would take it that it is intended to preserve the rights of all parties as they -exist under the New Brunswick statutes, whether any action has been taken either by lawrsuit or in any other manner.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: It seems to me that would be pretty hard to work out, because parties may have acquired a certain status by certain actions or steps that they have taken.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: Does the Bill reserve to this company the tolls which are provided by the British North America Act?

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext:
The tolls under this Act are to be levied by by-law of the company year by year, and the by-law has to be approved by the Governor in Council.
On section 11, subsection 3,-

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: I propose to make a slight amendment to subsection 3, by inserting. after the word ' river,' in line 11, the following words: 'or the floating down the same of rafted logs.' There was a question in the minds of certain gentlemen in the county of Bonaventure as to whether they would have free access to float their logs down the river if they chose to do so themselves. Under the provisions of the different sections, all the logs that are turned into the river and are floating in the river, must be driven by the company paying the company whatever rates or tolls are levied according to the bylaws. But in order to make it sure that the owner of the logs can raft his logs and take care of them himself, -we have suggested this amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: Has the hon. member given notice of this amendment?

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext:
No. But I may say that I do not think it is of sufficient importance to require notice. It has been drafted by Mr. Speaker and myself. The member for Restigouche (Mr. Reid) who is not here -at present, is interested on one side of the river and Mr. Speaker on the other side of Mr. CARVELL.
the river, and they have agreed that this amendment should be inserted. I do not think that the committee will feel that the matter is of sufficient importance to require the necessary notice. It is only done for the further protection to the small owner along the river who may have a few thousand feet of logs which he wishes to bring down himself, and not be subject to the tolls of the boom company.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext:
The amendment seems to be in the public interest.
Mr. DEPUTY" SPEAKER. I presume I mav accept it as not being of serious importance, and in the absence of opposition.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: It can be inserted by unanimous consent.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext:
I would ask the Minister of Public Works if he has given attention to this section to see that it properly protects the interests of the public on this navigable river; I am not prepared to say that it does not. I see there is a provision in it that it should be submitted to the Department of Public Works for approval.
Mr. PUGSLEY". I think the clause is in the usual form, which has been adopted in incorporating boom companies. A provision is made for handling logs by the company, and the tolls are to be submitted to the Governor in Council for approval. The amendment which the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) proposes, reserves the right to individaul owners to take care of their own logs if they wish to do so.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext:
I may explain for the benefit of the committee, that this enterprise up to the present has been carried on entirely under a charter of the New Brunswick legislature. The increasing importance of the lumber trade in that district has rendered it necessary to utilize both sides of the river. It is expected that this year 125,000,000 feet of lumber will be floated down the Restigouche river, and application has been made to this parliament by this company for better facilities under a Federal charter. I have received an important petition signed by some 400 residents of the * county of Bonaventure asking that the rights of the public and the rights of the riparian owners along the river should be protected. I went to the Private Bills Committee and asked that a sub-committee be appointed to discuss the Bill. This was done and clauses 24, 25. 26, 27 and 28 were inserted at my request for the protection of the riparian owners and the free navigation of the Restigouche river. This amendment which is now under consideration was inserted at my request to remove all doubt that the main channel of the Restigouche river would remain open to the public, that no obstruction of any kind will prevent the free navigation by all

interested parties. This company is practically a combination of all the large lumber merchants of that district. The lumberman who commands 100,000 feet of timber becomes de facto a member of the company. The small farmer cannot become a member, but by this Bill his rights_are protected under the understanding that his logs are rafted under the same rules as any other logs. Three points were insisted upon by me and were assented to by the member for Carleton: first, the free navigation to the public generally; second, payment by the company of all damages incurred by the riparian owners either to their property or fishing rights, because the Restigouche is probably the most valuable salmon fishing river in eastern Canada, (the payment of damages is well protected, because the company cannot enter into any works of any kind without first giving security in the courts of the district for damages that may occur); third, the initiative in the arbitration proceedings would have to be taken by the company so that the farmers in the district would not have to face a powerful organization. I think that all things considered, although we do not obtain all we ask, we have a fair protection for the people of the district. I have several letters from people on both sides of the river, saying that as far as they can judge at present the rights of the public are fairly protected under this Bill.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: Does the Bill leave it perfectly open to any one to drive logs down this river?

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: No. If any owner of logs drives logs on the river within the driving limits, that is from the mouth of the Red?wick river down to the boom limits, they must be driven by the corporation, and the owner must pay tolls.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: Are the tolls regulated in any way?

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: By by-law which must be ratified by the Governor in Council.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: I understand that the member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) explained that the object of the amendment which he inserted this morning was to reserve the right to any person to raft and drive logs provided the logs were rafted and not set loose. No operations are to be carried on in this river without some uniform system. If the farmer will raft his logs he is allowed to drive them, but if he wishes to have them driven that must be done by 'the company and he must pay the company.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: Are the operations on the Restigouche intended to be carried on in the same way as similar operations have been carried on in the St. John river?

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext:
They are almost identical, in fact this Act is almost a copy of the amended or consolidated St. John river Act, which was passed three years ago.
On section 20,-compensation and damages for not removing logs. Logs stored to be sold after public notice, if default in payment of assessment.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: It has been stated that provision is made in the Bill that tolls should be subject to regulation. Will the tolls under this section 20 also be subject to some regulation? *

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: This is only to provide in case the owner of the logs fails to take away his logs in proper time. The hon. member (Mr. Lennox) will understand that if twenty-five or fifty million feet of logs are left on the hands of the boom company after being rafted, the company would be practically out of business, for they would have no storage room. To compel owners to take away their logs within seven days., it is provided that the company should have the right to sell them on giving due notice, and to take from the proceeds sufficient to pay rafting, booming, and incidental charges. But I take it that these are all covered by the section providing that the by-laws are to be approved by the Governor in Council.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext:
I thought that, under this section, they were given the right to charge for delay. The Bill says the company may-
-sell so mucli of the said logs as should be sufficient to pay the amounts due upon such assessments together with the extra cost of storing the said logs and the expense of keeping them and of the sale thereof and all other incidental expenses.	-
I think the provision is a proper one, so far as 1 know, but I fear there is danger that exorbitant charges might be made. Is it not possible they might keep the logs longer than seven days, and make the charge accordingly? And would this be covered by the provision with regard to the regulation of tolls generally?

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: I can only say that the question has never been raised. Section 19 provides for an agreement or arbitration between owners and directors as to assessments. So, practically all the cost after the logs go through the boom are provided for under this section.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext:
This, I understand, is to provide in case the owner is probably in default. But cases of that kind might arise in which little or no moral blame would attach to the owner. Of course, I speak without knowing the proportions in this matter. I do not know what the storage for seven days on a given quantity of logs
til 75

would represent. Of course, if it is a very small matter, it is not worth discussing.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext:
1 think that under section 10 it is all provided for. Section 10 provides that the company may make bylaws fixing and regulating tolls and for the government of the company's affairs, but no by-law is to come into force unless and until it has been approved by the Governor in Council. I think this would cover all cases that might arise.
On section 21-Liability of company for logs lost by neglect: Logs lost otherwise to be secured at owner's expense.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: Is there anything in this section that makes the loss of logs prirna facie evidence of neglect on the part of the company, or is that left open?

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: That is left open. This is a very rapid river in the spring and, no matter what precautions may be taken, there is alwavs the possibility ot logs getting under the booms by the force of the current. But, unless the company have been negligent in the ordinary sense, they would not be liable, and the question of fact as to negligence is to be decided in each case.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: But there is nothing stated making the fact of loss a presumption of negligence which the company would have to rebut?

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext:
No, that is not specifically stated.
On section 26, expropriation of lands and rights.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext:
I beg to move that subsection 2 of section 26 be amended by inserting the wrnrd ' fishing ' between the w'ords ' the ' and ' rights ' in the 36th line thereof. I may explain generally that this section 26 recognizes the right of the fisher-.men along the shore to proprietary rights in the foreshore or even beyond the foreshore. I think there is a doubt in the law as to whether there are these rights or not. However, the lumbermen are willing to allow him these rights and to pay him for them, leaving the amount to be determined by arbitration. But there was a fear on the part of some of the riparian owners that if these provisions were made too broad the company might expropriate fishing rights and then lease them or use them for fishing purposes. The intention of subsection 2 was that the company might expropriate these fishing stands or rights only to be used for the purpose of their undertaking, and that they would not have the right to use them for fishing purposes. The word ' fishing ' was omitted from the 36th line, and it would look,there as if they could use them for any purpose Mr. LENNOX.
whatever. As amended it will read that they may expropriate these rights ' only for the purpose of the exercise of the company's owm business and without right to the company to continue to exercise any of the fishing Tights so acquired.'
They can use the locus for their own business, but they cannot use it for fishing. That is the object of inserting the word ' fishing.'

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: Do you not think that this will conflict with the rights of the province, if they have any rights, to control the fisheries along inland streams or lakes, or with federal rights, if there are any such rights?

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: I realize that the question might possibly arise, hut if we have no jurisdiction to grant rights, of course, no damage will be done. For a great many years, farmers along the shores have been fishing at certain places which they call fishing stands. They have obtained licenses yearly from the federal government and in the last year or two from the province of Quebec. The company are willing anyway to recognize that the owner has some rights, perhaps, by long usage-you might call it a prescriptive right-and they are willing to pay for them whatever they may be. I realize the point raised by the hon. member for East Grey, but I do not think any difficulty will arise therefrom. This parliament certainly would have the right to control the foreshore, and the land to be used as a booming privilege really is the foreshore of the Restigouche river, or below the mouth of the river along the bay and the harbour.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext: I would like to ask the promoter of this Bill if he is satisfied that the riparian owners down there made no objection to this subsection 2 of section 26, and whether the company will have the right to expropriate their fishing rights under this Bill? This is a very valuable salmon fishing river.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext:
They have objected very seriously for a long time, but the fishermen have all been offered a certain amount of money for whatever rights they might possess, in many cases amounting to thousands of dollars. The company altogether have offered the riparian owners something like $30,000 for their rights. In most cases settlements have been made. There are three on the Quebec side and six or seven op the New Brunswick side who have not yet been settled with. Every individual party was represented before the committee by Mr. Trueman, who used to be, judge of Probate in Albert county. He is now living in Dalhonsie. This clause was darfted by Mr. Trueman himself and inserted in the Bill by the committee exactly as he requested it to be. Therefore,'

this clause is really a clause drafted by the fishermen or the riparian owners- themselves.
On section 31; security for damages.

maintopic: RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY.
speechtext:
I gave notice the other day that I would move an amendment to be inserted as a new subsection of clause 28. It is as follows:
The costs of any arbitration under this Act shall be borne by the company, whether the same awarded is greater or less than the amount offered by the company.
The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Car-veil) pointed out to me this morning that it was provided in this Bill that expropriation would be carried out under the Railway Act and that there is a clause in the Railway Act which says that if the company is condemned to pay more than it offered, the company must pay the cost of the arbitration. The hon. member (Mr. Carvell) who has legal training, says this amendment would be contrary to the prevailing jurisprudence, therefore I am not insisting, but this is the very cause of the difficulty between the riparian owners and the company. Wherever the parties have been able to agree, the riparian owners have been bought out. The Busteed estate, for instance, have sold out to the company. The riparian owners thought that the company should in any case be compelled to pay the cost of the arbitration, but if this principle is contrary to the jurisdiction it should not be insisted upon, and I will, therefore, withdraw the amendment. Of course, I make a great distinction between a railway and a river in regard to expropriation.

Bill (No. 159) to amend the Exchequer Court Act.-Mr. Aylesworth-read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is a Bill which has been passed by the Senate in amendment of the Exchequer Court Act.

Would this extend to any such line, leased line, or line taken over by the Intercolonial? The Bill refers to the Prince Edward Island railway explicitly, thus making a distinction there. But we have passed an Act giving the power to take over other lines. Would the Bill cover these lines also?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I can only say that if these lines fall within the description of the Intercolonial or Prince Edward Island railway, the liability would exist, but not otherwise. This Bill is limited to the construction, maintenance or operation Mr. AYLESWORTH.
of the Intercolonial railway and the Prince Edward Island railway.

Suppose, for instance, that, by the leasing of some line, the Intercolonial were extended to Georgian bay. That leased line would become part of the Intercolonial system, but would it be a part of the Intercolonial railway under this Bill? It seems to me there might be a difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am afraid I am not able to say what view the court might take of the position of a leased line. Much might depend on the special terms of the lease under which the road was being operated. One line might be held to fall properly within the description of the Intercolonial railway, and another might not. The special circumstances in each particular case would have to be considered by the court if the question arose.
. Mr. SPROULE. Why would it not be proper to apply it to the whole system as well as to a portion of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can only say that I did not frame this Bill. It has come from the Senate, and has been the result, from what I have seen of the proceedings there, of a good deal of discussion. It was introduced in quite a different form, and ultimately took the form in which it is now before us. I have not had the advantage of any discussion with the gentleman who introduced it in the Senate, but simply have taken charge of it when it came to this House, because it was a measure relating to the disposition of legal matters.

I would like to have an explanation of the position which this Bill occupies as regards the government. It is introduced as a government measure, and is listed here under the head of 1 Government Orders.' I understood-and I do not know whether other members of the committee have understood it in the same way -that all the Bills that come to us in this way are government measures, though they may not have been introduced in parliament by the minister whose names they respectively beaT. For instance, I imagine that when we had a Bill under the name of the Minister of Justice, that meant that it was a government measure originating with the government and particularly, as a matter of actual detail, originating with the Minister of Justice. I was going to ask about that before any statement had been made by the minister. The minister said this Bill was passed by the Senate with certain objects. He further makes that clear by saying in the end:
I have not framed this Bill: it was introduced by a gentleman in the Senate.
I think he said in effect that it was nut in his name. That may be a proper prac-

tice, I will not say it is not, because I have not had sufficient experience to pronounce upon it, but I am prepared to give my idea about it. I would not have thought it was a proper practice. I do not understand that it is proper or can be proper that a Bill should be presented to this House to all intents and purposes marked as a government measure,, as something that has originated, say with the Minister of Justice, be brought in as a government measure, get its place in this committee as such, have precedence as a government measure, and yet not be a government measure. That is what this is. It originated with some individual in the Senate more or less responsible'-probably less- and it is then fathered by the Minister of Justice for better or for worse. It evidently does not fill the condition it ought to fill for the reason that,, as the minister admits, it may not cover, it probably does not cover, the whole government system of railways. As my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) has pointed out, there is no good reason why it should not cover the whole system; if it is a good measure it ought to apply to the whole system. So we have the minister putting through a Bill that is not his own, except for the accidental circumstance here adverted to. It is not as bad as the minister forcing through, for instance, the St. Lawrence Power Transmission Bill, but it does not seem to me to be right, and I would like to have an explanation and to know if that is a proper practice. It is not tlje only Bill placed under similar circumstances among the government orders. Whether the others are in the same condition or not I do not know. There are one or two in the name of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The remarks I made a moment ago were in answer to the question of the hon. member lor East Grey (Mr. Sproule) as to whether this Bill did not extend to other lines of railways than those mentioned on the face of the Bill. I gave the exact and accurate answer to that inquiry. I did not frame the Bill, the Bill was introduced into the Senate,, not as a government measure, but by a member of the Senate who is not a member of the government. It was passed by the Senate in its present shape after much discussion. I have moved the second reading of it and adopted it as a measure which I am quite prepared to father and for which I am quite prepared to take the responsibility. If any hon. gentleman thinks it does not go far enough he is at liberty to move an amendment, and if that amendment is carried by this House it will go back to the Senate as an amendment so made for the consideration of that body. But this Bill as it stands is one that I present on behalf 197
of the government as an extent to which the government is prepared to go in this matter.

This does not meet the case. The point is that there must be some fair treatment of members of the House and of the Senate. A private member introduces a Bill very much in the public interest, recognized at least by the public as in the public interest, or a senator may do so, but he cannot get it through. Is it right that fish should be made of one and fowl of another, and that the Minister of Justice or another minister of the Crown should take up a private Bill and give it that precedence that it has by reason of being a government Bills, introduce it into this House, put it among government orders and not say a word about it unless such words as may accidentally fall from him in the course of discussion. It seems to me that this kind of thing will lead to a very serious abuse. It is not treating the House fairly to introduce a Bill in that way without an announcement to that effect, and the mere statement that the minister is prepared to assume responsibility for it does not meet the whole question. Supposing that the government have a perfect power to do this kind of thing, I doubt the expediency, the propriety or the fairness of such a course. I do not think it is giving a fair chance to members of the House and of the Senate to stand on equal terms. If the government will say that they will take every Bill introduced by a private member and put it through the House after the time at which public Bills introduced by ordinary members can be put through, well and good, but to leave it in the position that supporters of the government, members who have the sympathy of the government, can get Bills through and others cannot, is not fair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: my hon. friend will not be surprised if I tell him that measures which might have merit in his eyes might have no merit in mine.
There is no doubt about it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is a measure which has merits in the eyes, 1 believe, of my hon. friend and of the government also, and for that reason it has been adopted by the Minister of Justice, who thought he was doing a good thing in adopting it. I think my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is the first to agree with him. The only criticism of that hon. gentleman was that the measure did not go far enough. I am prepared to say there is a good deal to be said in favour of the contention of my hon. friend from Grey, but the Minister of Justice did not consider whether or not it went far enough; so far as it goes-, it is satisfactory to every one in the House, and I think for that reason it ought to be adopted.

I think it unfortunate that we should leave the measure with the anomaly that an action may be brought in the Exchequer Court with regard to damages on one portion of the Intercolonial Railway system and not with regard to damages on another portion, so that there is redress for a sufferer on one portion and not on another.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The criticism of my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) is right; for my part, I agree with him. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ayles-worth) has said nothing to the contrary. He said that he would not be prepared to say that the Bill would not cover the case put forward by the hon. member for East Grey. I am giving my own judgment. I would not put my opinion against that of the Minister of Justice, but, as I understand it, the moment a line of railway is leased by the government and brought under the administration of the Intercolonial railway, it would be covered by this legislation. The Minister of Justice has had more experience in these matters than I have had, and he would not go as far as I in expressing his opinion, but if it were to turn out that I have taken too sanguine a view of the matter and that this Bill does not cover the point of my hon. friend, I see no reason why we should not extend it later on.

I think we should make it plain now.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide for a revision and amendment of the Currency Act, chapter 25, of the Revised Statutes.
Further resolved, that the standard for gold coins of the currency of Canada be such that of one thousand parts by weight, nine hundred shall be of fine gold and one hundred of alloy; and the standard for silver coin shall be such that of one thousand parts by weight nine hundred and twenty-five shall be of fine silver and seventy-five of alloy; that the standard weight for gold coins of the denomination of ten dollars in the currency of Canada be two hundred and fifty-eight grains, and the standard weight for a silver coin of the denomination of fifty cents be one hundred and eighty grains, and for other gold coins and silver coins proportionate weights respectively; that the Minister of Finance be authorized to issue out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund such sums as _ may be necessary for the purchase of bullion in order to provide supplies of coin for the public service ; and that the cost, charges and expenses incident to carrying out the provisions of any Act founded upon these resolutions be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This resolution is a necessary step towards the introduction of a Bill to revise and amend the Currency Act. The amendments, while necessary, are not very, important, and I have no reason to suppose they will be contentious.
What do the proposed amendments amount to?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The main change is to enable us to carry out the intention of the government to provide a gold currency for Canada. There is a provision in the existing law for a gold currency, but it is found not to be very workable. The currency of Canada is on a gold basis, and as we all know, the British sovereign has the standard value of four dollars eigthy-six and two-thirds cents. We have in reality a second gold standard, the difference being so slight that it has not hitherto been deemed necessary to call attention to it. As a matter of fact the American gold coins are legal tender in Canada, and for ordinary purposes it is the American gold coin and not the British gold coin that is used in Canada.
How are the American gold coins legal tender in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They are, and have been for many years, legal tender under our Currency Act.	There being thus
two gold standards it might naturally be assumed that they would be proportionately the same value, but they are not exactly the same. There is a fraction of dif-

ference, not large enough to affect commercial transactions, but large enough to demand consideration in a Currency Act. If we should make the Canadian five dollar. gold piece on the basis of the British sovereign at the value of four dollars eighty-six and two-thirds cents, we would be producing a coin intrinsically of less value than the American $5 piece, and as we have, like the United States, a decimal coinage, it would be manifestly inconvenient if our $5 gold piece should be intrinsically of less value than theirs. The effect of the change is that we shall make our $5 gold piece of just a trifle more value than it would he if we made it on the basis of the British sovereign. Therefore, the American $5 gold piece and ours will be intrinsically of the same value. It would no doubt be found convenient in time that these coins should be interchangeable across the border, although I do not know that our American neighbours would likely make ours a legal tender as we did theirs. Perhaps the time may come when we shall no longer need to make the American gold coins a legal tender; but it is legal tender now, and the trade and commerce of the country has found it advantageous. We propose to make the gold coin of Canada of a quality, weight, fineness, &c., which will correspond exactly with the American gold coin.
What would he the exact value of the British sovereign upon the same basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The difference is very fractional. We shall still recognize the British sovereign as four dollars and eighty-six and two-thirds cents, and I think the actual value is four dollars eighty-six cents and some-small fraction. The difference is so small that it will not affect ordinary transactions, hut in a Currency Act we must take notice of it. Another point is that if we were to make a $5 gold piece on the basis of the British sovereign, four dollars and eighty-six and two-thirds cents, we would have a coin which in weight could only be expressed in most inconvenient decimals. It is advantageous that the weight of the coin should be such that it can be conveniently accounted for in all operations. These are the main changes although some few other changes are made for the improvement of the Act.
Resolution reported, read a second time and agreed to.
Mr. FIELDING moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 195) respecting the Currency.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice) moved second reading of Bill (No.
197i
138) to amend the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act.
Will the hon. gentleman explain.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The object of this Bill is to supply an omission from the present law on the subject. The statute relating to the protection of customs and fisheries, chap. 47, Revised Statutes of Canada, provides that in the case of a seizure of goods, or of a ship, every penalty or forfeiture may be recovered, or enforced in the Exchequer Court, on its admiralty side, or in any Superior Court in the province, within which the cause of prosecution arose. Pursuant to that provision of the statute the Exchequer Court has promulgated its rules of procedure, but some of the provincial courts, and possibly all of them, have net done anything of that nature. The result has been that when proceedings to enforce a penalty or forfeiture of this character have been instituted in provincial courts there has been no practice laid down by any rules which could be followed, and such proceedings have, in consequence, in some instances, proved nugatory, and the advantage of being able to resort to provincial courts has been thus practically taken away. This Bill proposes to remedy that defect by adding as a subsection to the section I have referred to, a provision that in so far as there are no general rules made by the Superior Court of any province, the practice and procedure in cases of this character in the provincial court shall be regulated by the practice and procedure for the time being in force in the Exchequer Court.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time, considered in committee, reported, read the third time, and passed.

Sir FREDERICK BORDEN moved the second reading of Bill (No. 194) to amend the Militia Pension Act. He said:	This
Bill is based upon resolutions which were explained and discussed very fully in Committee of the Whole.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 6B, subsection (e),

This is a new provision, and is the most important provision of the Bill. It is proposed to allow an officer who is transferred from the active militia to the permanent force, to count on retirement one half the time he has served in the active militia up to ten years and not more, though

he is not to count that service at all until he has served ten years in the permanent force. It is often very desirable to utilize in the permanent force the services of officers who have distinguished themselves in the active militia, but such officers have been very slow about entering the permanent force, because no portion of their time of service in the active militia counted for a pension, and very often they would not think of going into the permanent force until they had reached the age of 45 years or over, so that it was impossible for them to secure a pension, the minimum service for a pension being 20 years. But under this provision, an officer of the age of 50 who has distinguished himself in the active militia, say a lieutenant-colonel could come into the permanent force and serve his ten years there before reaching the age of 60; and if he had served 20 years in the active militia, he would be entitled to count ten years of that service, so that at the age of 60 he would have 20 years' service to his credit, and be able to retire with a pension. It is thought to be in the public interest that this should be encouraged, and we believe it will be greatly to the advantage of both services.
Is there any definition of the word ' force '?

Yes, it means the permanent force.
On section 2,

Subsection 2 of section 12 of the Militia Pension Act reads as follows:
Time served in His Majesty's regular forces may be counted towards a pension in the case of non-commissioned officers and men transferred to the^ permanent force in connection with the taking over by the government of Canada of the garrisons at Halifax and Esquimalt.
To that we add,
And in the case of such non-commissioned officers and men as have been or may hereafter be transferred from His Majesty's regular forces to the permanent force under arrangements made between His Majesty's government and His Majesty's Canadian government as to the pensioning of such non-commissioned officers and men.
It is simply extending the application of this provision to the non-commissioned officers, and men of the British army who may come into our force, it allows their time to count. At present the men do not contribute towards the pension, neither here nor in England. As a large number of our permanent force come from the British army, it is convenient to draw our men from that force. The object of this provision is to enable us to give due consider-Sir FREDERICK BORDEN
ation to such men, and an opportunity of counting the time which they have served in the British army.
What are the arrangements referred to?
That would be by order in council, or exchange of despatches between the war office and the colonial office, and this government.
Have any arrangements been actually made, or does this refer to arrangements that may be made in the future?

I think the arrangements are now pending.
On section 3,
This includes our own men who have served in South Africa, and other places, applying the same rules that apply to the officers.
Does time count from the date they are first enlisted in Canada, in the case of the South African men?
I think so.

In subsection (e) of 6B section 1, what do these words mean,
' half the time served in the active militia other than the force?'	*'

That means the active militia. The active militia strictly includes the permanent force, the permanent force is a branch of the active militia; so those who have served in the permanent force are already provided for. This is providing now that service in the active militia shall also be counted to the extent of one-half.
But the word ' permanent ' is not there.

Where the word ' force ' in the Pension Act occurs it is explained to mean the permanent force:
(e) Time served in the employment of the government of Canada in connection with the militia stores of Canada prior to the organization of the ordnance stores corps.
What does that mean?

Formerly the men who served in what is now known as the ordnance stores served as civilians. They were men really too old to enlist in the ordnance corps when the ordnance corps was established, and it is thought that their time ought to count, and that they should receive a small pension. There are only some half dozen such cases.
You do not include officers of the Northwest Mounted Police Force. Why do you make that distinction?

We do not include time served in the active militia, either. The men of the Northwest Mounted Police do not contribute to the pension fund, only the officers contribute, and the same' way with the permanent force.

It is the officers I am speaking of. You say time served in the Royal Northwest Mounted Police shall be included in the time of service of an offi-. cer for the purposes of the Act, and when you extend this clause of section 12 of the old Act, you do not include them, although you include all the others.

The reason it was not included in section 3, I think, is that section 3 deals only with men, and not with officers. But the principle my hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) raises is as to the service of the men in the Northwest Mounted Police. As I understand the point, it amounts to this-that if you give to officers the advantage of including time which they have served in the Northwest Mounted Police, why should you not give to men the advantage of the time that they have served in the Northwest Mounted Police?

I do not think the condition is likely to arise as regards men. The Act has been very carefully drafted to meet all the requirements of the department, and I feel sure that it does so. I can see no Teason why the Northwest Mounted Police might not be included, but I feel sure it is unnecessary. However, I will look into that matter. The Bill might be allowed to go through, and it will be very easy, at another session of parliament, to amend it if necessary. But I am sure it is mot necessary.
Why should not it include non-commissioned officers and men who go into the permanent force?

It will in this way: If a man who has served in the active militia, in the ranks or as a noncommissioned officer, should join the permanent force and be promoted to the rank of a warrant officer, then his time would count. But I think it would be very im convenient-there would be so many difficulties in proving service-and very undesirable that we should count the time of men as privates in the permanent force who have served as privates or non-commissioned officers in the active force.
How about the man who has been sergeant-major in an infantry regiment for a number of years, and who goes into the permanent force and becomes a sergeant?

If he should join the permanent force and be promoted.
as he undoubtedly would oe, to the rank of a warrant officer, when it came time to pension him, his time served in the active militia, if he could prove it-and undoubtedly a man of that class could do so-would be counted towards the pension.
There are so few promoted to be warrant officers, it seems hardly fair.
A great many are appointed warrant officers.
I would ask if, in the Pension Act, there is provision for pensioning non-commissioned officers and men?

Yes. And non-commissioned officers and men are not called upon to contribute in any way. The officers contribute five per cent annually-it is deducted from their pay. But non-commissioned officers and men who have served twenty years are pensioned without having contributed anything.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that the regulations of the 21st day of June, 1909, intituled: ' Regulations of the National Parks of Canada/ which were passed on the date above mentioned by His Excellency the Governor in Council, under authority of section 4 of the Rooky Mountains Park Act, being chapter 60, R.S.C., 1906, copies of which regulations, as well as the necessary order in council, have been laid before this House, are, in so far as they relate to the Rocky Mountains Park of Canada, approved by this House, in accordance with provisions of subsection 3 of section 5 of the said chapter 60.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This resolution is required in order to give legal effect to the amendment and consolidation of the regulations governing the national park which were passed last year under authority of council. The original regulations under which the national park is controlled were passed many years ago, and, of course, before the park had been in operation. Since that time, it has been found that in certain particulars they fell short of the requirements, and in other particulars they were perhaps, a little in advance. So, after many years of enforcement there was a general amendment and consolidation which we now ask the House toi give effect to. The provision of the National Parks Act is that regulations which are passed and given effect to in the first place by the Governor in Council must be endorsed by parliament in order to be

maintained in effect. The principal changes that are made include the following:
The reservation of a strip of 100 feet along all bodies of water in the park.
Changes, mostly of a verbal nature, are made in clauses relating to erection of buildings, defacement or removal of natural objects, trees, structures, &e., and also providing for the seizure and disposal of any timber, minerals, &c., taken unlawfully.
New clauses are added regulating the use of fire in the open air which was not covered by the old regulations. They require precautions in using fire, and make provision for proper equipment of locomotives and clearing of railway right of way. These clauses are similar to those adopted for the forest reserves.
A new clause provides that camping parties must clean up camping grounds before leaving.
For the villages in the park, regulations are made requiring connection with the sewer, preventing loafing on the streets or obnoxious or disorderly conduct.
Changes in details are made in regard to pasturage and hay so as to make the regulations work satisfactorily. None are of special importance.
Changes are made in the dues for sand, stone, gravel and lime, reducing them slightly.
Hot Springs: The change is a provision suggested by Mr. John Galt, civil engineer, that no further licenses for the use of water from the Hot Springs should be granted except by special order in council.
A number of additional occupations and businesses, such as restaurants, theatre's, circuses, &c., have been brought under the license system so as to secure fuller control. The regulation for licensing guides for camping parties has -been enlarged so as to place more responsibility on guides and place them under more control.
Sale of liquor: It is merely provided that liquor shall not be sold without a license. This leaves out additional provisions of the old regulations which are better covered by provincial legislation.
Persons in the Dark are required to answer inquiries of rangers or game guardians and livery stables, and outfitters must keep records open to rangers of parties sent out by them.
It is provided that dogs shall not run at large; that no firearms shall be kept or carried, except by duly authorized game guardians, unless properly sealed; that there shall be a right of search where game is suspected of being had in possession unlawfully; that not more than fifteen fish shall be taken in one day and none less than six inches in length. The appointment of game guardians is provided for.
The Rocky Mountains Park Act provided Mr. OLIVER.
an extreme penalty of $50 for violation of regulations. The old regulation reduced this to $20. It is considered that $50 is not too large a penalty for serious offences.
The new regulations have been in force since the beginning of last summer and have been found to meet the requirements. Of course from time to time amendments will have to be made, but our experience is that the amendments contained in these regulations were necessary and desirable, and we are asking the House to confirm them.

I submitted these regulations to some of my friends who are more familiar with these matters than I am. I do not think they are in the House to-day, and perhaps the minister will allow this to stand until to-morrow. What is the general policy of the government in regard to the leasing of portions of these parks for residential purposes? Is it purely a matter of application and arrangement with each individual person who may desire to procure a lot, or are the properties disposed of by public auction, or in some such way as to give equal opportunities to all persons who may desire to avail themselves of such privileges?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The policy, of course, is that there shall not be any general acquiring of residences throughout the park; it is a reservation for the benefit of the public, and of course in its very nature it is not intended to be dotted here and there with occupation. So, the policy of the government is not to allow residences to be established except in definite locations where they will be most convenient, and where they will be most required. A person would not be allowed to establish a residence in some attractive place in the park simply because he desired to do it. It is felt that the natural beauty of the park should be preserved. To allow occupation the townsite of Banff is laid out, and within that townsite the lots which have been surveyed are leased at a certain fixed rental for a fixed term of years. There is no competition, the rentals are scheduled, and whoever wishes to apply for a lot gets it on the application, and on the conditions as to residence and construction, and observance of the laws, &e. that are contained in the lease. Canmore, a coal mining town, I think was established before the park was set apart, so that there is private ownership of property in some portions of Can-more, but so far as the jurisdiction of the government is concerned, the lots are leased. Some time ago an amendment was made which permitted the government to sell lots in those towns, but so far that provision has not been availed of, and all the lots are under rental in both Banff and Canmore. Bankhead, a coal mining

town, is under the control of the Canadian Pacific railway, but . the principle there is the same. Wherever it is found necessary or desirable to permit residence, as in the case of these towns, a survey is made, and the lots are leased for a term of years under certain conditions and rental. Outside of this, permanent occupation is not permitted.
As I understand, the opportunities for application are the same to all persons.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, yes.

The rules are general rules applicable to all persons who may desire to acquire one of these lots.
I presume there are restrictions as to the character of buildings, &c.?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course in the beginning when the town was laid but it was not desirable or possible to impose any serious restrictions, and as a consequence some parts of the town of Banff are perhaps not quite what might be desired. But under the administration as it is now, permission is only given for buildings of a certain size, and character, and the lessee must conform to the regulations in the matter of obeying the rules laid down or his lease is forfeited.

Has the minister considered whether he has any jurisdiction in making regulations in reference to the protection of game, other than what the proprietor or a person having the fee simple to that land would have?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
I would like to ask the minister if the policy he has just enunciated in regard to the disposition of lots for residential purposes in this national park is also applicable to the forest reserves. There are some very desirable locations in some of these forest reserves. For instance, in the Riding Mountain timber reserve, Clear lake is a beautiful lake, it is free of timber, and I am aware that several persons have applied for lots for the purpose of having summer cottages.
Is this policy for the disposal of lots for such purposes applicable to forest reserves in the same way as it would be in the national park?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I might explain that the purpose of the reservation of the Rocky Mountains park is entirely different from the purpose of the forest reserves. The reservation of the Rocky Mountains park was for the purpose of pleasure. It was placed under reservation to be used by the people of Canada, and those of the rest of the world who wished it as a pleasure park, and so, in our regulations, control and administration of the Rocky Mountains park, we contemplate the presence of people, the coming and going of people, in, we hope, very large numbers; whereas, the forest reserves were set apart without having in view the presence of people. Rather the absence of people was in contemplation, the object being to secure the growth, preservation and reproduction of timber. So that, the policy .of the one is entirely different from the policy of the other. At the same time the question that my hon. friend has raised does exist, or is raised, in regard to a number of forest reserves, and I may say that we propose to measurably apply the policy regarding pleasure parks to certain parts of the forest reserves such as the case which my hon. friend has mentioned. We propose to do something of the kind with regard to the reserve that was created at the Waterton lakes in the Rocky Mountains near the international boundary line. Wherever, in any forest reserve, some portion is found that can be used for pleasure purposes without endangering the general purposes for which the reserve was set apart, it would be the policy of the government to take such measures as would meet the case. I am not able to say whether special legislation will be required or not. I am not sure whether the provisions of the Forest Reserve Act would permit us to make an arrangement such as that which applies

to the Rocky Mountains park, but it is a matter of detail. If we are not permitted to do that by the Forest Reserves Act as it stands at the present time I have no doubt that the House will agree, in due course, to legislation that will enable us to do so.

Does the minister remember the terms on which the park was taken over, and does he remember whether there was a declaration that it was a work or a reservation for the general benefit of the people of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have not the Act in my
hand, but I am satisfied that there was such a declaration.

Well, that may alter the argument a little, but if there were not something of the kind the local government could not convey their power of legislating with reference to game on that particular portion of their territory, and regulations in reference to game would be void.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is an arguable question. Even although the park was set apart for the general advantage of the people of Canada, and I am satisfied that the Act so declared, I am afraid that the provision was not carried forward into the Autonomy Bill creating the province of Alberta. But, it is recognized to be desirable from all points of view that the game should be protected, and that it is necessary, and desirable that provision for actually taking care of the game should be made, and should be made by this government in pursuance of its policy of preserving the park as a pleasure resort. While friction might arise, I think the probability is very distant; certainly it has not arisen, and I do not think it is likely.

I would think that the proprietary rights of the Crown in the right of Canada would be ample enough to give them jurisdiction to make some regulations at least. I would be a little surprised to find that there was any declaration such as that to which the minister alludes, because I do not see how a park could be declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. It seems to me that that would be a very unusual declaration, because the word ' work ' has no such meaning in the British North America Act. But, inasmuch as the government of Canada would have the right, by virtue of its proprietary interest, to exclude any person from coming within the limits of the park, I suppose it might qualify the right to enter the park by means of regulations; in other words, it having the right to exclude altogether, it could give the right of admission subiect to certain regulations, and perhaps

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: that might be sufficient to justify the regulations which the minister has made, although I have not examined the subject with any great care.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have been very careful. We have recognized that our position is not established as one of absolute control, and therefore we have gone carefully, and with due regard to the game protection policy of the province. I am satisfied that we have sufficient jurisdiction to create a good deal of friction if we wanted to. We do not want to, and I think the House may rest assured that the provisions we are asking it to assent to, and the administration of those provisions will guarantee that there will be no friction.

T would like to inquire of the minister about the Kootenay lakes timber reserve. The minister is aware no doubt how beautiful those lakes are, and there is a great desire on the part of many people to build there. I would like the minister to inform me if the applicants can get permits to build in or about the Kootenay lakes. It is probably a timber reserve although I am not quite sure to what class it belongs.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The answer would practically be the same as that I gave to the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche).
I mentioned the Kootenay lakes reserve as being a forest reserve, not a park reserve, but it is of a class in which it would be very desirable to permit a part of it to be used as a park reserve. It is our policy to make such arrangements as are necessary to that end. We may need special legislation, but if we do not we will make provision without further delay. However, these regulations have no application whatever to any other than the Banff park.
Under the present regulations can a person obtain by lease or in some other way a site around the Kootenay lakes to erect a building?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think there is some provision whereby building privileges can be secured. In reply to my hon. friend (Mr. J- Haggart) I may say that section 3 of the Rocky Mountains Park Act reads:
Said tract of land is hereby reserved and set apart as a public park and pleasure ground for the benefit, advantage and enjoyment of the people of Canada, subject to the provisions of this Act and of the provisions hereinafter mentioned, and shall be known as the Rocky Mountains park, Canada.
Progress reported.

Bill (No. 186) to amend the Irrigation Act was read a second time and the House went into committee thereon.

On section 1,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The matter of drainage is being dealt with by the provincial governments and there are applications which are of a very minor character in respect to which it is unnecessarily burdensome to require plans to be filed in all cases as the existing statute provides. Under this, instead of requiring plans to be filed in all cases they need only be filed when the Minister of the Interior considers the work of sufficient importance to demand them.
On section 2,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Act as it now stands contemplates the reservation by the minister, of land which it is desired to use for reservoir sites, or for the right of way of irrigation canals. We propose to add to that the right to expropriate in case some part of the area desired to be taken as a reservoir site may have passed into private hands. Of course, the holding of one small piece of private property would defeat the purpose of the government in making a general reservoir.

If you own the lands you have the right to reserve them, but the minister is taking power here to expropriate, for the purpose of irrigating a section of the country, land which may be vested in the provincial government. Is the minister quite sure he can do that constitutionally?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman may be quite correct, but that view is entirely new to me. This parliament has declared that all the rights to all waters in the three prairie provinces shall be vested in the Crown in the right of the Dominion. The right over all waters in the three prairie provinces was vested in the Crown in the right of the Dominion, and the Acts providing for the establishment of the new provinces have preserved that right to the Dominion.
Do the Autonomy Acts reserve to the Dominion all the water rights over both navigable and non-navigable streams?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, as I understand the matter. At any rate, I am not presuming to establish the fact either one way or the other. I merely desire to amend the legislation which is on the statute-book, whether it is constitutional or otherwise, and I am saying that when we take the power to reserve, we should, in order to make that power effective, also take the power to expropriate.

As I understand, what the minister is endeavouring to accomplish is this. There may be a certain tract in one of the western provinces which it would be eminently desirable to reserve
for water storage, for irrigation canals and ditches; but it may have happened that before the importance of that proposal was recognized by the department, some portion of that land may have been alienated and homestead rights upon it may have been granted. This legislation is to permit the government in such cases to acquire that land by expropriation in order that the proposal may be carried out in exactly the same manner as would have been possible except for that alienation.	-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is an absolutely correct statement of our position.

I understand that that is the object of the minister, but I very much doubt the power to carry it out.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.
Mr. PUGSLEY moved that the House go into committee on Bill (No. 103) to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
Will the minister explain the object?

The two sections of the present Act, which it is proposed to appeal, are sections 4 and 5 of chapter 115 of the Revised Statutes. Section 4 is as follows:
No bridge, boom, dam or aboiteau shall be constructed so as to interfere with navigation, unless the site thereof has been approved of by the Governor in Council, nor unless such bridge, boom, dam or aboiteau is built and maintained in accordance with plans approved by the Governor in Council.
I propose to enlarge the scope of that by including in it the words: ' wharf, dock, pier or other structure of any kind.' Then I propose to leave out the limitation expressed by the words: 'so as to interfere with navigation,' and to provide that none of these structures ' shall be built or placed in or across any navigable water, unless the site thereof has been approved,' &c. The object of the change is to give to the Governor in Council a larger measure of control over navigable waters and over works which may be constructed in, upon or across such waters.
Will that apply to those already built?

No, only to the future. It is a curious fact that as long ago as 1870, parliament passed an Act relating to the Ottawa river which gave the government absolute control over all works on that river in these words:
The navigation of the River Ottawa, as well by vessels and boats as by rafts and cribs of timber or logs, is hereby declared to be sub-

ject to the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, and all canals or other cuttings for facilitating such navigation, and all dams, slides, piers, booms, embankments, and other works of what kind or nature soever in the channel or waters of the said river, or in which the waters of the said river are used, and in whatever province situate, and whether constructed or to be constructed, and whether constructed by the government of Canada or by the government of the late province of Canada, or by the government of Upper or Lower Canada, or by any private party by the consent and authority of any of the said governments, which shall, from time to time, be recognized by the Governor in Council, on the report of the Minister of Public Works, as being or as having been, constructed- for any purpose of public utility, shall be held to be works for the general advantage of Canada, and, with all works of like character, no matter by whom constructed and whether being recognized as being for the general advantage or not, situate in or on the waters of the said river, shall be subject to the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, and shall be under the control and management of the Department of Public Works, and subjeot to the provisions of the Act, intituled, ' An Act respecting the Public Works of Canada/
That -does not apply to wharfs.
It -says piers.
Those piers are for the purpose of facilitating the passage of timber down the river, and are not to be utilized as wharfs.

The word pier is often used to mean whaTf. Moreover, this says, 'and other works of what kind or nature soever,' which would surely include wharfs. I quote this only to show how far parliament went with regard to the Ottawa river; but, strange to say, with regard to other navigable waters throughout Canada, the only provision is one applicable to a bridge, a boom, a dam or an aboiteau, there being no reference whatever to wharfs or other structures which might be as objectionable in navigable waters as any one of these four works which the section refers to. Another objection to this section is that it limits the power of the Governor in Council to eases which actually interfere with navigation, and the question would naturally arise as to who shall be the judge as to whether or not a particular work does interfere with navigation. As I mentioned when the Bill was being read a second tinfe, in quite a number of cases the provincial governments have erected bridges across navigable rivers in cases where I think it would he proper that they should come to the department at Ottawa for approval of their plans. But they have contended that these bridges do not inter-Mr. PUGSLEY.
fere with navigation, that is, they take the ground that in some cases, while the river is navigable, it is not navigated, and, therefore, their works cannot be said to interfere with navigation. My attention has been particularly called to the case of a bridge which was built across the South Saskatchewan river by the Alberta government. There is no draw in the bridge. Their action was followed up by telegraph and telephone companies which strung wires across the river. A little later on an enterprising citizen living further up the Saskatchewan river concluded he would build a tug boat. He started down the river with it, and got entangled in the wires and by the bridge, and the result was that his boat was wrecked, and the unfortunate man lost $9,000 or $10,000 worth of property, and apparently has no redress against anybody for the damage he sustained. I think it is in the interest of the countrv generally that, as the Dominion parliament has control of navigation, it should have control of works of whatever nature or kind that may be placed in navigable waters, and that parties proposing to erect bridges, or wharfs, or booms, or anything which may prove an obstruction to navigation, should come to Ottawa and file their plans with the department and get approval thereof. If, in the opinion of the engineers, the work would not unreasonably interfere with' navigation, there is no doubt the approval would be granted. I may mention a case that occurred recently in respect to the harbour of Victoria. The Grand Trunk Pacific were proposing to construct a wharf in connection with their steamship service to the city of Victoria. They fortunately seemed to recognize, what a great many other people and companies recognize, that they ought to come to the Public Works Department, even although the statute is silent on the question of wharfs. They came to the department and their plans were sent out to the resident engineer. He naturally consulted with the .public bodies there, like the harbour association, the board of trade, and the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and the general opinion was that if the wharf were built as the Grand Trunk Pacific proposed, it would seriously interfere with the navigation of the harbour, it would seriously interfere with the handling of the steamships of the Canadian Pacific railway. Consequently the engineer reported against allowing the wharf to be built as proposed, the Grand Trunk Pacific consented to alter the plan, and the Canadian Pacific railway and the hoard of trade consented, and in that way the whole difficulty was overcome. I only mention that case as an instance of the desirability of having the plans of any structure obstructing navigable waters, submit-

ted to the department for approval. Section 5 of the old Act, strange to say, is limited to bridges, it simply says: 'any bridge to which this part applies.' We desire to substitute the following:
Any work to which this part applies, which is built upon a site not approved by the Governor in Council, or which is not built in accordance with plans so approved, or which, having been so built, is not maintained in accordance with such plans, may be removed and destroyed under the authority of the Governor in Council.
Why, in section 4, some four different classes of work should be mentioned, and why, in section 5, only one of these four classes should be mentioned, I am unable to understand.
Does this apply only to works to be built?
Only to works to be built in future.

How does the minister construe the words ' navigable waters '? Does that mean that no obstruction of the class mentioned in section 4 proposed to be amended, shall be built without the authority of the minister or of the Governor in Council? In the case of a reach, or a bay, which leads out to a navigable water, and which is not in itself navigable, would this Act impose upon any one proposing to construct a pier or a bridge for private use, the necessity of applying to the Governor in Council for permission?
No, it is limited expressly to a navigable water, structures which are proposed to be built upon a navigable water.

The Bill which the hon. gentleman proposes, I fear, may go a good deal further than he really intends. I have drawn his attention already privately to a matter in my own county. Along the shores of Lake Ontario, the waters are constantly washing away the land, and deep erosions have been made in the shore, so much so that in one instance I was informed by a former owner of the land that an apple tree growing 120 feet from the shore 25 years ago, has now entirely disappeared. That means that 120 feet of land on that farm has been washed away in the course of 25 years. In other places, roadways are interfered with, and there is a danger that land will have to be acquired to provide new roadways to supply the place of the travelled road which possibly has been in use from 75 to 100 years. Even in the village of Burlington, where a government property is only a short distance from a deep erosion across the street, there is danger that before many years the government will have to acquire another drill hall, or they will have to do something in the meantime to stop the destruction of the
shore by the waves. Now the plan that is being adopted by the farmers and the municipal council is to throw out groynes or docks, or wharfs, from 75 to 100 feet into the lake, with the idea that the waves will wash the silt and gravel in upon these docks, or wharfs, or groynes, and in that way accumulate or build up more land, instead of constantly washing it away. The hon. gentleman has been in a position to expend government money for the purpose of protecting this shore. So far, he has declined to do anything, and I am afraid that if we wait too long the destruction may-reach very great proportions. The municipal council of the county of Halton. has. already taken the matter up and has built one of these groynes out into the lake, 75 or 100 feet, and I believe it is having very good effect in preventing further washing away, in fact, it is perceptible already that new land is going to form and that the destruction of property will be arrested. Nor is that an uncommon thing. I am informed that farmers along the shore, in order to protect their land, are building little wharfs as they see the need of them. They build a crib and fill it with stones- a very simple matter, but it has the desired effect. Now, it is going to be a very serious problem for these people if they have to run down to Ottawa and get the consent of the Governor in Council before thev are permitted to build a little crib filled with stone for the protection of their own land. The government will not do anything for them, and here the hon. minister passes a Bill to make it as troublesome as possible for them to protect themselves. I think the Bill is a mistake, that the law was well enough before. The broadening of the law as proposed by the hon. minister is only going to cause additional trouble to the people who desire to protect themselves, and whom the government does not seem willing to protect. I think it is a pity that the wording should have been broadened, and I hope the minister will revise the Bill and put the law back just about where it was. I am sure the minister does not wish unnecessarily to injure property or to prevent people from protecting their property. He may have in view wider cases and larger circumstances and may not have thought of these apparently small matters, though matters of very much importance to the men to whom I refer.
