I am sure no difficulty or hardship will arise in the case to which the hon. member (Mr. Henderson) refers. The matter of throwing out groynes to protect the shore is a matter in which no minister would interfere, unless it were found, in some way, to cause an interference with navigation. When this Bill was before the House on a former occasion, the

hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Barker) and I discussed it across the table. The difficulty is to put in an amendment making exceptions. I am sure the matter pan be well left to the good judgment of the engineering department of the government, and to the minister from time to time. There will be no disposition whatever to interfere with works of the character to which the hon. member refers. But it is important that the construction of wharfs should be as much under the control of the Public Works Department as the construction of bridges. The proceeding will be a simple one. In cases in which the work is at all extensive, it ought to be submitted to the department. To such small works as the hon. member refers, there will be no objection on the part of any reasonable minister, or of any officer of common sense

But suppose a party, say, on the St. Lawrence, or on any of the lakes, erect a wharf without coming down to Ottawa for the purpose of having it approved-a wharf for a little island cottage, for which, of course, it would not be worth while to make an application-what control would the party who built it have over it under this Act? He would have no right to erect it, and any person would have the right to tie up to it or even to remove it if necessary. The builder of it might even be liable to indictment at the instance of any person who had a grievance against him. The difficulty is the annoyance to which people might be subject. Of course, the case of building a bridge over the Saskatchewan is a different matter. They had no right to build such a bridge without getting the authority of the Public Works Department. The same would apply to the erection of any work of sufficient importance at the mouth of the St. Lawrence, or at any other of a hundred other places in Canada. But the application of the principle to everything in the shape of a wharf, is objectionable.

Let me illustrate the point I wish to make by citing a case which came under my own personal observation. Some years ago in the province of New Brunswick, the provincial government erected a bridge across the St. John river, and put a draw in it which, they contended, was sufficient for the purposes of navigation. The premier and attorney general at that time, Mr. Blair, said that, as the bridge did not interefere with navigation, he would not go to the authorities at Ottawa but would build the work according to plans satisfactory to himself and his government. But I say that, in the general interests of the country, the local authorities ought not to control such matters. The Governor in Council should be the judge, and the Department of Public Mr. PUGSLEY.
Works should be the advisers. As to the small wharfs that have been referred to, I am not quite sure what their position is now. The soil under navigable waters, in most cases, belongs to the federal or the provincial government. Therefore, if a man builds a wharf in navigable waters, even in front of his own property, he is trespassing upon somebody, he is doing an act which is unlawful, either against the Dominion government or against the provincial gpvernment. This applies to ninety-nine cases out of a hundred.
Would these wharfs be liable to common usage by the general public, not having the authority of the Crown?	[DOT]
No more than they are now.
They may be now.
Yes, they may be, it is difficult to say. Many wharfs have been built in navigable waters illegally. I really do not think there will be any practical inconvenience or injury from this Bill.

The minister is departing from the terms of the statute in force for many years. The statute originally provided that:
No bridge, boom, dam or aboiteau shall be constructed so as to interfere with navigation, unless the site thereof has been approved by the Governor in Council, nor unless such bridge, boom, dam or aboiteau is built and maintained in accordance with plans approved by the Governor in Council.
The minister proposes to substitute a provision that:
No bridge, boom, darn, aboiteau, wharf, . dock, pier, or other structure of any kind, shall be built or placed in or across any navigable water, unless the site thereof has been approved by the Governor in Council, nor unless such bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau, wharf, dock, pier or other structure is buiit and maintained in accordance with plans approved by the Governor in Council.
I do not know whether the term ' navigable water ' has been defined in the statutes or not?
No, it is the first time.

There -might be some difficulty in giving that word an exact application. We know what the words ' navigable water ' mean in Great Britain, there have been many cases defining the expression there, but on this continent the expression has varied from time to time according to the particular conditions of the locality, and the particular purpose for which it is proposed to use the water. For example a river may be navigable for one purpose, and absolutely unnavigable for another. I do not know whether the ex-

pression ' navigable water ' would have the same meaning in every province in Canada. It is not defined in the statute. I suppose it must be left to the determination of the courts in each province, and I would think some difficulty might arise. Apart from this statute altogether in the case alluded to by the Minister of Public Works there would be no right to build a wharf or any other structure so as to interfere with navigation, and even if the person building that wharf absolutely owned the soil by virtue of a grant from the Crown that would not entitle him to build a wharf upon it. In the harbour at Halifax that very question arose twenty-five years ago in the case of Essen vs. Wood. There was a grant from the Crown in the right of the province to one of the citizens of Halifax of certain lands below high water mark. That citizen extended his wharf so as to cover that land. An adjoining wharf proprietor went with a force of men, pulled up the piles and destroyed the wharf. An action was brought, and it was contended that such person was justified in destroying the wharf, because although the person building the wharf had a title from the Crown to the land in question, that person was not entitled to use the land in such a way as to interfere with the right of navigation which was common to all subjects of His Majesty. An appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada brought a decision that by reason of the fact that the wharf so constructed was an interference with navigation, the person destroying the wharf was justified.^ The ground of that decision was that the Crown in the absence of legislative sanction has no right to authorize any man to interfere with navigation. An Act of narliament is necessary for that purpose. Thus the statute with which the minister is dealing is in one sense an enabling Act and not a restricting Act.
Hear, hear.

I suppose we can consider all these matters when we get into committee, but I would invite the minister's special attention to his use of that expression * navigable water,' because I am inclined to think some confusion might arise in different provinces from the use of that expression unless it is defined.

Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the Bill.
On section 1,

I would call the attention of the committee, and especially of the leader of the opposition whose remarks on the subject are very valuable, especially when he speaks of this Act being an enabling Act, rather than a restricting Act, to the wording of the Railway Act. The Railway Act speaks particularly of a railway crossing a navigable river, and requires that application shall be made to the Board of Railway Commissioners, as well as to the Minister of Public Works. In that case I do not know that there has been any definition of the words ' navigable water '.
It would be rather difficult to frame a definition.

Very. Of course there is a difference between what would be called a floatable stream, and a navigable stream. A floatable stream, down which logs could be floated, would not be considered a navigable water. The courts of New Brunswick have decided that such a floatable stream is a public highway for the floating of logs, but not a navigable water, as it would be construed under this Act. Section 233 of the Railway Act provides :
When the company is desirous of constructing any wharf, bridge, tunnel, pier or other structure or work

These words are about as broad as the words of the Bill I am asking the committee to consider.

in, upon, over, under, through, or across
any navigable water or canal, or upon the beach, bed or lands covered with the waters thereof, the company shall, before the commencement of any such work,-
(a) in the case of navigable water, not a canal, submit to the Minister of Public Works, and in the case of a canal to the minister, for approval by the Governor in Council, a plan and description of the proposed site for such work, and a general plan of the work to be constructed, to the satisfaction of such minister.
Now, in effect I am asking in regard to all navigable waters that practically the same law may be enacted as section 233 of the Railway Act enacts so far as similar works constructed by a railway company are concerned. The leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) very truly says that this is an enabling Act, rather than a restricting Act; it is enabling the Minister of Public Works, or the Governor in Council to make legal the erection of wharfs and other works in navigable waters. I have a case in point. A person in British Columbia erected a wharf in navigable water, and some question, arose as to the legality of the structure. He applied to my department for approval, but I was obliged to say: No, I cannot approve of it, because you should have come before 'you undertook the construction of the work; the statute is limited to that; I cannot approve of a work already constructed, the Act says in a later section: Approval of the proposed work. The gentleman was very much astonished, and ag-

grieved that he could not get this wharf approved of.
There is no remedy under this Act for him.

No, I do not intend to change that. That will be found in section 7, which says:
The local authority, company or person proposing to construct any work in navigable waters, for which no sufficient sanction otherwise exists, may deposit the plans thereof and a description of the proposed site with the Minister of Public Works, and a duplicate of each in the office of the registrar of deeds for the district, county or province in which such work is proposed to be constructed, and may apply to the Governor in Council for approval thereof.
You will see it is limited to work to be done in future and, therefore, under this section, I felt that I could not approve of a work already constructed. No doubt the effect of the statute would be that when a wharf was once approved of, it would become legal, whereas, otherwise, it would be illegal.	*
Does the minister think he has no jurisdiction at all on navigable rivers at the present time as to what character of wharf, bridge or anything else may be constructed thereon?

That is a pretty large question. By the British North America Act the parliament of Canada is given control over navigation. I would think that probably the minister could apply to the Minister of Justice and have an injunction issued to prevent interference with navigation but that might lead to litigation. I think it very desirable to have some defined plan of operation laid down by statute, which persons would be obliged to follow, so that every man, when he was proposing to erect a structure in a navigable water, would know what he had to do, and if he got the approval of the Governor General in Council he could proceed and no individual could afterwards complain that his structure hindered navigation and was therefore illegal.

I do think that the expression 'in navigable waters' perhaps might work out in the way suggested by my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson). If you provide that these structures shall not be built or placed in such a way as to interfere with navigation, that is one thing, but if you provide absolutely that they shall not be constructed in navigable waters, that is another thing. They might be constructed in navigable waters in such a way that they could not possibly interfere with navigation. Some of the illustrations given already would serve as examples of that. A Mr. PUGSLEY.
man, for instance, might be protecting his own property. He might be obliged to build a structure for the protection of his property in navigable waters.

Who should be the
judge of whether it does interfere with navigation or not? Suppose it is not navigable water should not the Governor General in Council be the judge of that?

The remedy is a very plain one. If any man builds a structure so as to interfere with navigation without statutory authority enabling him to do so, any one coming along, whose right to navigate is so interfered with, can tear it down and destroy it. It is a public nuisance. Therefore, it seems to me there is absolute protection in that regard. But, if a man places a structure for the protection of his own land in such a way as not to interfere with navigation he harms no one, and he is not put to the trouble and expense of seeking from the Minister of Public Works an authority which under the premises is not at all necessary in the public interest.

What is an interference with navigation? Suppose, as in the case to which the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) referred, a man builds out into a navigable water for 100 feet from his own shore another man comes along with a row boat or a tug boat and says: I want to navigate the water where that pier is-is not that an interference with navigation?
Yes, and he would tear it down.
Is that desirable? Should there not be some authority which should settle these things?

I understand that the federal government has set up a claim that the Horseshoe Falls at Niagara is a navigable water. Does this Act pretend to set up the claim that every water-fall where a dam can be built, or where a water-power can be developed, comes under the jurisdiction of this government?
This is limited to navigable waters. I do not know whether the place to which my hon. friend refers is navigable or not. I rather understand that it is not navigable.

I think the minister should state in the Bill what the term 'navigable water' means. The hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) claims that the falls on the Nipigon and Pigeon rivers are navigable. They are navigable only for a Peterborough canoe drawing perhaps three inches of water. If that constitutes navigable water

it will give this parliament complete jurisdiction over all such streams in every province of the Dominion. To make it move effective this clause covers all the water-powers that are supposed to be under the jurisdiction of the provinces. The Bill says:
No bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau, wharf, dock, pier, or other structure of any kind, shall be built or placed in or across any navigable water, unless the site thereof has been approved by the Governor in Council, nor unless such bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau, wharf, dock, pier or other structure is built and maintained in accordance with plans approved by the Governor in Council.
Not only the actual work but the site of the work must be approved of by this government. That places the site of every power in every province in the hands of the Dominion. I am not prepared to go quite that far, and I would ljj^e the minister, before this Bill passes, to make it clear that there is no intention to interfere with the Tights of the various provinces in their own water-powers. For instance, the province of Ontario has passed an Act whereby every power of 100 horsepower, but I understand it is 100 horsepower-in the province of Ontario, it does not matter who is the owner of the land, or what the navigation of the stream is, or whether that power is developed by a company or any individual, is subject to the right of the province, in which the franchise is vested and which charges 50 cents per horse-power per annum. I would like to be satisfied that the Bill does not take away or interfere with the rights of any of the provinces in their own water-powers, their rights in their water-powers being as well established as their rights in their lands, forests or minerals.
This Bill is intended only to interfere with the navigable waters.
What constitutes a navigable water?

I think Mat there is no question but what the term ' navigable water ' would mean a water which could be navigated by fair-sized boats-such boats as would carry traffic, freight and passengers. A stream which would float a canoe or a log might be floatable, but it would not be navigable. I would have no objection, if any hon. gentleman thinks he can give a definition of navigable waters which would he better than the definition which the court has made, to our defining what ' navigable water ' means. I do not know that it has been defined by statute in Canada, although the courts have defined it as a body of water which can be navigated by sailing vessels or steam boats. I think that a stream through which a rowboat could pass should not be regarded as a navigable river within the meaning of a statute of this character.

Does subsection (b) of section 13 of chapter 115 throw a little light on this question of what is or what is not a navigable stream in its definition of the word 'vessel'? For the purpose of the Act, the word ' vessel ' is defined as being ' any description of ship, boat or craft of any kind whether propelled by steam or otherwise.'
That is contained in the part of the chapter relating to the Marine Department

Precisely. But when they define waters which are navigable, as the waters mentioned in that Act, does not the minister think that a court would seize on that subsection for a correct interpretation of the word ' navigable '?
I would hardly think so.

There should be some definite description of what navigable waters mean before this clause is passed. There is an Ontario Act providing that in the unorganized districts of the province there shall be 66 feet reserved on each side of any navigable water, and it has been decided that any water that floats a canoe is navigable water under that definition.
Has that been decided by the courts in Ontario?

My hon. friend (Mr. Arthurs) refers to the Rivers and Streams Bill. It would be well to put in an interpretation clause stating what under this Act would be construed as navigable water. For instance, as far as the purposes of the Dominion are concerned, I should consider that if a stream entered into provincial rivers or international waters any part of that river from its mouth would be navigable as far un as navigation could be had without obstacle. But the ramifications of this Act are so extensive that it would cover that stream to its source. We have had it held in this House by a gentleman who is very much interested in these power Bills that any stream at all which empties into international or interprovincial waters is a navigable stream to its source for the purposes of this Act, and that the Dominion has complete control over any river or stream tributary to any of the great lakes or the River St. Lawrence, We would save a great deal of trouble in the future if we define in this Act what a navigable river is. I have no doubt the intention is to prevent an obstruction being put in a navigable river, such for example, as the Kaministiquia at Fort William, without the consent of the government. I should think that a river, or that part of it affected, should be taken over by procla-

mation before it could be considered as under the jurisdiction of the Dominion. We all know there has been a decision of the courts in the question ol the ownership of streams in the province of Ontario under the old River and Streams Bill.
Would my hon. friend send me a memo as to where I can find that case?
It is a famous case which was fought through to the Privy Council by Sir Oliver Mowat, and I think it had reference to a large branch of the Ottawa river.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the Caldwell and Maclaren case.

I understand the hon. gentleman to say that it had neen decided by the courts that a navigable river was a river along which any kind of a vessel, even a row boat or a canoe could be propelled. I do not see how that question could arise in the Caldwell-McLaren case.

It was I who made the statement that the Ontario government had raised such a contention, and I said that there was an Ontario Act under which one chain perpendicular width was reserved along all navigable streams. The provincial government has interpreted this to mean any streams which are at all navigable.
I understood the hon gentleman to say that it has been so interpreted by the courts.
No, but the Ontario government issues their patents with this reservation regarding all these small streams.

I can assure the committee that my whole desire is to limit this to what are in reality navigable waters, and hon. gentlemen will see how desirable it is that there should be federal control ever the structures which are to be built therein. I am not prepared to say whether it would be possible to define navigable waters for the purposes of this Act, but I would be glad to receive any suggestions from any hon. gentleman as to a proper definition.

The Muskoka lakes empty into the Georgian bay by the Muskoka or Moon river. These lakes are virtually in two sections, and there is a lock built between Rosseau and Muskoka lakes with a fall of 4 or 5 feet, and that lock is maintained by the province. A line of steamers plies up and down the lakes. At the lower end of the lake there is a dam maintained by the Ontario government so as to keep the lakes at a special level, and Mr. J. A. CURRIE.
the total length of navigation on these lakes must be 80 or 90 miles. Under this Bill the control over these waters would apparently be taken over by the Dominion. The same is true of the Maganatawan; there are 15 or 20 miles of navigation from the mouth, then rapids for 25 miles, then another long stretch of navigation on that river. The same conditions are to be found on the Nipigon and on the Columbia and Kootenay rivers in the west. The minister should endeavour to find some definition which would end this continual friction with the provinces, and which would clearly distinguish the rights of the Dominion and of the provinces in these navigable waters. The time of parliament has been wasted a great deal with these continuous disputes, and they are not in the interest of the provinces or to the credit of the Dominion. I should hope that no one in this parliament would want to infringe on the rights of the provinces.
This simply deals with the control of navigation and does not touch the rights of any province.

In the riding I represent the tourists have wharfs almost at every island on these lakes, and under this Bill these gentlemen would have to send down a plan or specification of each small wharf to the government. I do not think that is the intention of the minister, and I think some provision should be put in the Bill which would eliminate that difficulty. It seems to me to be manifestly unfair.

Yes, if this Act had been enforced, it would in the ordinary course of events have prevented the very difficulty to which my hon. friend has referred. The petition which he has read shows the necessity of having some oversight- over these navigable waters, so that persons, before erecting any structure, would know that it was their duty under the law to come to the Minister of Public Works and submit plans for the structure, so that they could be inquired into by the engineers, and if they showed no interference with navigation, they would be approved of. The difficulty to which my hon. friend refers would, I think, be obviated if this Act were in force. [DOT]

I may inform the hon. minister that most of the present property owners have bought their lands within the last ten or twelve years, and these lumbering operations have been going on for a good many years. I would be glad if this grievance could be remedied in some way. All that these petitioners ask is that a gap be made in the booms whereby they could have ingress and egress to and from their cottages along the shore.

If my hon. friend will be good enough to write me a letter on the 198
subject, I will give directions to have it looked into.
I do not think that this Bill would remedy the grievance, if ' navigable waters ' is to have the definition the minister gave a little while ago.
These booms are on the Ottawa river, which is navigable. The logs come down the Petawawa river, and the cottages are right at the mouth of that river on the Ottawa river.

The difficulty in the past has been that there has not been enough attention paid to the right of the public to navigation. Men have erected booms, bridges, wharfs and piers, in many cases without the slightest regard to the public interest. In the very case my hon. friend from North Renfrew has referred to, lumbermen built booms and dams in the river knowing that the riparian owners had a right to navigation. We find the same thing all over the country. There is nothing in this country that we ought to guard more sacredly, in the interests of future generations, than the freedom of navigation, and parliament ought not to be afraid to entrust the matter to the engineering staff of the department and the Governor in Council, which of course would only act reasonably upon the reports the engineers would make.

So far as I am concerned, with my knowledge of the facts, I cannot consent to this Act passing in its present form without a protest. The hon. minister cannot show the House a single complaint or petition to his department from any person in any province of the Dominion asking him to take the absolute control of all navigable waters. The old Act read that as long as the bridge, boom, dam, pier or other structure did not interfere with navigation, it could be built. The minister goes far afield and provides that nothing can be built on any navigable water without the approval of the Governor in Council. I will warrant that there are two thousand small wharfs on the Muskoka lakes, built by private individuals, costing anywhere from $25 to $1,000. The same thing exists all over the country. Arc these people to be compelled to come and get the consent of the Public Works Department and to file plans made by an expensive engineer and costing more than they are worth, although very often these structures are miles away from any interference with navigation? The very stream the hon. member for North Renfrew speaks of is under the jurisdiction of the province of Ontario. There are streams where the province has given boom companies the rights to build booms and sluices and carry on their works. There are millions of dollars invested in these boom companies in the province of Ontario, as I have no doubt



there are in Quebec and other provinces. The hon. minister proposes to lord it over all these investments and to the men who have built extensive booms in accordance with the regulations laid down by the province. He steps up with a great club and says, we have taken these under our control and protection. The great awakening for the protection of the navigable waters of the country has taken place first in the provinces, and the work cannot be done as successfully at Ottawa as it can nearer! home. A man in British Columbia would have to come to Ottawa to get the permission of the Department of Public Works to build a $35 dock.
Therefore I think the minister should modify it, and leave the clause just as. it was before. If the minister can show this House any documentary proof of need, or any petition asking him to pass this Act, then I would be willing to stand aside. But there has been no public petition presented for it in the House. The hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. White) has a petition, but he will find that the Ontario law covers his case. They can compel any company that is booming logs to leave a gap for vessels. All that is required is that somebody should call the attention of the government to any obstruction that may exist, but they have gone to the wrong quarter. I think the minister in that Bill is endeavouring to take away the rights of the provinces. I do not hesitate to say that to my mind it is one of the most vicious attacks on provincial rights that has been made in any Bill that has been brought before this House for a long time. Whilst he may say that he can do this, that, or the other thing, the fact remains that those who are looking for those powers and approvals can already go to the provinces, and now he wants to give them power to come here, and thus keep this House in a turmoil for weeks. I think for the sake of peace it would be in the interest of the public that the old clause should remain as it is, and that before any such drastic change as this is made, the provinces should be notified that it is the intention of the federal government to take charge of all these dams, booms and sluiceways. The provinces have officers of their own appointed to look after these things, and they are paid for it, and they are doing their work satisfactorily. The minister intends to have a double jurisdiction. I think the Act is highly objectionable.

There is another thing I would like to bring to the attention of the minister. In the province of Nova Scotia, for example, all along the shores of the coves, and small harbours, fishermen living on these shores have in many cases a little wharf or jetty; and the lobster factories along the coast usually have some-Mr. .1. A. CURRIE.
thing of the same kind to enable the lobster fishermen to bring in their catch, and land it at the factory. It seems to me that under the provisions of this statute every one of those fishermen would be required to file plans for every little wharf or jetty that he builds in connection with his occupation. No doubt the minister does not intend anything of the kind, but I think that will be the effect of it. As has already been suggested, it seems to me that the mischief he seeks to prevent could be avoided by using the expression which is to be found in the former statute, and for the reason very forcibly pointed out by my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie). If, for example, he would add after the words ' navigable water,' the words which are found in the present statute, ' so as to interfere with navigation,' would not that be quite sufficient to prevent the mischief which is sought to be prevented? I think it would. I think it would be dangerous to depart from the expression which has been found fairly sufficient to safeguard the public interest in the past.
IMr. PUGSLEY. The only object is to make the law in regard to all navigable waters the same as it has been for nearly forty years with regard to the Ottawa river. There has never been any serious difficulty I ever heard of on the Ottawa river as to the law being oppressive upon riparian owners. My hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie) rather speaks as if this Bill is proposing to invade provincial rights, because we propose to take more control over navigation. Well, it is not this parliament that is now proposing to do that, because the British North America Act has already given to this parliament control over navigation.
I said navigable waters, not navigation.
Navigation usually takes place in navigable waters.
There may be no navigation in navigable waters.
Wherever a water is capable of navigation, I think it is our duty to preserve the right of navigation upon it for the people of the country, for the benefit of transportation interests.
I suppose the point is that a navigable water should be capable of being used by the owner in such a way as would not interfere with navigation.

Then the question is what authority should judge as to whether it interferes with navigation or not. The hon. member for Simcoe says that the provincial authorities in Ontariojiave given permission for the erection of booms, and

other structures in navigable waters. Well, they talk about encroaching on provincial rights, I say that if they have done that they have encroached in the most flagrant manner upon the rights of the Dominion parliament, because this parliament is the only authority that can give a right to erect structures on navigable waters, that power is absolutely, by the British North America Act, vested in this parliament. Now I desire, as I am sure hon. gentlemen, opposite desire, that the Bill should be made as workable as possible. I am dis-[DOT]posed to consider the suggestion which the' leader of the opposition has made. I do not know whether the Bill will fairly accomplish the desire which I have to preserve navigation, by putting in the clause he suggested, but I will be glad to consider it. I do not think this is a matter which could be determined off-hand; therefore I would move that the committee report _ progress, and the matter can be reconsidered before we resume consideration of the Bill in committee.
Mr. J- A- CURRIE. The hon. minister need not go away with the impression that I was endeavouring unduly to oppose, this Bill. I wish to point out the difference between this^ Act and the old Act. Under the old Act, if any one put an obstruction in a navigable water that interfered with navigation, a complaint could be made to this government, and the parties could be compelled to remove the obstruction. I think that is only fair and just, and that is a right given to this parliament under the British North America Act. But to go wider afield, and to say that nothing can be placed in a navigable water without getting permission from this parliament, is quite another thing. Very often the ownership of the land under that water is vested in individuals, individuals have riparian rights, and the right of the owners of the lots extends out into the water; and to say that they cannot put a small dock in there although it may be twenty miles away from navigation, to say that a small fisherman in New Brunswick must come here, and pay $40 or $50, and deposit plans before he can put a twenty foot dock on piles at which to land his boat, or that the owner of a summer cottage in Muskoka who wants to put a little wharf on the edge of the lake where he can embark in his motor boat, must come down here and file plans, and the same all along the St. Lawrence river and every other inland water,-why the hon. gentleman would have to have a staff of 400 or 500 men to look after all these matters. For that reason I say the clause is absurd. The only right that is given to this parliament under the British North America Act is the right to prevent any interference with navigation, but 198i
that does not mean that this parliament has the right to take control of all rivers streams, and lakes in the country, as this Bill proposes to give them.

I presume that this Bill would cover government docks which, in their present position, are somewhat of a menace to navigation. I have in mind particularly the dock at Petawawa. This case I have brought to the attention of the House on several occasions. The minister will remember that I wrote him last fall with reference to this dock, stating that the^ passenger steamer on the Ottawa river, plying between Pembroke and a point forty-five miles west, was almost stranded on a sand-bar quite near the dock. It seems that the dock has not been built in the proper place or that, in any case, the river should have been dredged at the dock. I have here a letter in reply to the one which I wrote to the minister:
Department of Public Works,
Ottawa, November 2, 1909. Gerald V. White, Esq., M.P.,
Pembroke, Ontario.
Sir,-With reference to your letter of the orct September last, re dredging required at Petawawa wharf, I beg to state that an engineer of the department has been sent to Petawawa, and he held the matter in abeyance until he could make a survey which, he reports, cannot be done for some time.
From discussions which our engineer had with Captains Murphy and Tessier, masters of the passenger steamer ' Victoria/ the local slide master and personal inspection, that officer states that the sand-bar below the dook will require scraping next year at low water, the water this year being too high for scraper work. There is no dredge at present on these waters to attend to the dredging required.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant, NAPOLEON TESSIER,
Secretary.
Now, I think this is an urgent matter. On several occasions, the steamer 'Victoria' has been stranded on this sand-bar, endangering the life of passengers on board. It seems to me, therefore, a matter of this kind should receive the attention of the department. I do not see what reason there will be to wait until some time next August, when the water is low, to attend to the matter, for this steamer starts running as soon as navigation opens, and runs during the whole season.
Mr. PUG8LEY. How far is the Petawawa wharf from Ottawa?
It is about ten miles above Pembroke, which would make it about 110 or 115 miles from Ottawa.
I suppose that we are in the same position this year as we were last year in regard to a dredge in that locality. I will make inquiries.
I would like to have something done, for this is certainly a very dangerous spot.

I am very much interested in this Bill from the fact that, during the last session of the Ontario parliament, a company of which I am a member, applied to that parliament for authority to build some dams on the Mississippi river for the purpose of conserving the water. In years gone by,^ the lumbermen had the privilege of erecting dams at the mouth of certain lakes for this purpose. These dams have all disappeared, but the manufacturers in the different towns affected have formed a company for the purpose of building dams where the old wooden dams used to be. It is the intention of the new company to build cement dams. We had a Bill passed through the Ontario legislature at its last session to give us the power to build these dams. The question is, if the Bill now before us passes, how will it affect this company? As to this being a navigable stream, that is the question I would like to have defined. There are on certain stretches of the river, small steamers, but I do not know that they go as far as where we propose to build dams. And there, may be such vessels as gasoline launches or boats of that description plying on these waters. But, if we go to the expense of building these dams, and the question arises whether this is or is not navigable water, it may involve a heavy loss. This we would like to know before we go to the enormous expense involved in these works.

What is involved in the power proposed to be given under this Bill to ' remove or destroy all structures ' anywhere on navigable "waters? Is it the idea or intention, for the future, to prevent the erection of any dam, wharf or pier, on navigable waters of any kind? As the minister" probably is well aware, a great number of water lots largely throughout the province of Ontario, have been granted to private parties during the last fifty or one hundred years, so that practically the greater part of the foreshores of our lakes have been thus granted. For instance, in Toronto water lots were granted by the Crown many years ago, extending 600 feet out into the water. These lots are now' owned by private persons. In many cases the owners have built wharfs, boat-houses and other structures out toward the 600-foot limit-this limit, in many cases, extending far out into navigable waters. These lots have always been regarded oy the owners as their private property, just as much so as a piece of- land in the city. The whole water-front, of Toronto is built on water-lots originally granted by the Crown. They are filling in water-lots to-Mr. PUGSLEY.
day, extending the harbour out into the bay, and are building piers on what is supposed to be private property, believing that they have as much right to do so as a man would have to build a house on a city lot. The land is covered by water, but the owners have the exclusive right from the Crown and have so treated it at all times. As I read the Bill it would certainly empower the government-if the Bill is intra vires-[DOT] to remove any or all of these erections on these lots and to prevent in the future the erection of anything upon these water-lots on which there is navigable water. The whole measure is a very important one, a very serious one, and a very far reaching one, and I would ask if it is the intention of the government deliberately to extend the scope of the Act as far as I have indicated.

The only intention of the Act, as is apparent on its face, is to give to the Department of Public Works and the Governor in Council a control over the erection of structures in navigable waters. My hon. friend speaks of there being hundreds of wharfs built out into the navigable waters in localities with which he is familiar, and he asks if it is the intention of this Bill to have these removed. I say, no. This Bill will not 'be retrospective in its operation, but will only deal with the future, and it is important that persons who propose erecting structures in navigable waters shall come to the department for approval. My hon. friend knows, as a lawyer, that if any man, whether he come in a small boat or a tug boat along the water and strikes one of these wharfs and finds his progress impeded, he can go to a court and compel the removal of that wharf as being an obstruction to navigation, because it is illegal. A man may own the soil under the water, but he has no right to build out a structure into the water which in any way interferes with the right of every one of His Majesty's subjects to go wherever he likes in a rowboat, a motor boat or a steamboat, and any wharf built without legal authority in a navigable water is in that sense a hindrance to navigation and therefore illegal.
This Act, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L Borden) has said, is an enabling Act, and it enables the Governor in Council to approve of these structures. The only effect it has, and it is a very important effect as far as the public interest is concerned, is to keep a control over the structures, to regulate their building and to determine where they shall be placed. We cannot protect the interest of navigation and provide for the future interests of the people in that regard unless we have some control over the places where these works shall be constructed and over the manner in which they shall be constructed. That is the sole object of the Bill, and it

does seem to me there can be no objection to it. We do not desire to encroach on provincial rights or to interfere with water-powers, but only to secure the right to discharge the duty which under the British North America Act is- imposed on this government and which this government ought, in the interest of the public, to discharge as well as it can. My object in suggesting that progress should be reported was that I should give careful consideration to the suggestion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) as to making some amendment which would prevent the possibility-although I do not think it is a possibilitj which ought to be seriously considered- of the Act in any instance working with any degree of harshness. I would be glad to consider the suggestion, and if it is possible t-o make an amendment which would meet my hon. friend's view without impairing the efficiency of the Act and preventing it attaining the object in view, I would be glad to suggest to the committee that the amendment should be made.

Section 7 of the existing Act reads:
Such local authority, company or person shall give one month's notice of the said deposit of plans and application by advertisement in the ' Canada Gazette,' and in two newspapers published in or near the locality where such work is to be constructed.
This would work very harshly as regards summer tourists and the erection of small wharfs.

That section might be amended to provide that no advertisement need be published unless the minister should think it in the public interest. 1 would be glad to consider any suggested amendment of that kind.	-

The minister is right and wrong in part. 1 am not quarrelling with his Bill, I think it is highly desirable that people should not be allowed to impede navigation as they are now doing by erecting structures along lake and river fronts. It is quite true, as he points out, that in many cases grants from the Crown of these water lots are subject to the rights of navigation through the waters upon these lands, and in so far as those grants are . concerned, legislation of this nature would be applicable. It should properly apply to grants originally made in which the rights of navigation, were preserved and protected. In those cases, it would be quite right that the government should wish to regulate navigation, and the grant of land from the Crown being subject to that right, to pass an Act providing some machinery for enforcing that right. But, on the other hand, as the minister will recall, a large amount of our water front, in cities particularly, has been granted without rights of navigation, and in many cases
for acres or even miles, the foreshore and navigable water has been filled in to form solid docks and piers, where no right of navigation was reserved. When the Bill comes to be considered in detail1, it might be well to consider those cases, so that a proper distinction might be made between the supervision over cases in which the rights of navigation were reserved and cases where the grants were made not subject to that provision.

That is worth considering.

On section 1, incorporation.

Since this Bill was last before the House a good deal of interest-has been manifested in it, and a good deal of research has been indulged in by members, I presume, on both sides of the House. Owing to the very Conflicting nature of this Bill in connection with the St. Lawrence Power Company's Bill passed in 1901, I may say that it is the wish of of a great many hon. members on this side of the House that a little further time should be had to look into- the legal bearing of one Bill upon the oth^r so that the whole aspect of the case may be placed in view. I had hoped that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) would have been here, but in the absence of that hon. gentleman I think I voice the wishes of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House in asking that this Bill should stand over until next Monday. I think that possibly there will be time saved.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
I can see no object in the Bill standing. The primary objection to the Bill when it was under consideration before was that there might be some question that it would lead uo to the damming of the St. Lawrence. Granted even that the Bill at that time said so, which it never did, the amendment which has been introduced would absolutely prohibit anything of the kind whatever, so that the whole question of any danger along these lines is absolutely removed from the Bill by the amendment. I cannot see where anything would be gained by allowing it
I

to stand. There is nothing more that can be known of the Bill. In its present form it is simply a transmission line company, and it has absolutely no relation to the Bill of 1901 whatever, and even if it had it is absolutely restricted by the amendment proposed.

Whether the two Bills are not intimately associated is a question that a great many of the best legal minds in the country are in doubt upon; in fact, the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) frankly admitted when the matter was up before that the two Bills were associated together one being the. complement of the other. In considering the question of the amendment which is proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Pardee) further doubts have arisen as to the position that the company would then be in with relation to the damming of the St. Lawrence and with relation to the whole Bill.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman read the amendment?
Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Does he take any such meaning as that out of it? Does not the amendment absolutely preclude any such conclusion being come to?
I think not.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
The amendment is as follows:
Nothing herein contained shall be deemed to constitute an approval by parliament of any future development of water-power by erecting a dam in or across the St. Lawrence river under the Act 1 Edward VII., chapter 3, intituled: 'An Act to incorporate the St. Lawrence Power Company,' or otherwise. Nor shall the company hereby incorporated be authorized to transmit power generated by the St. Lawrence Power Company other than the power generated by and in connection with the works already constructed by the said St. Lawrence Power Company.
Nothing could be plainer in limiting the rights granted by this Bill than the language set forth in the amendment.
May I ask the Prime Minister if the government has had any correspondence with the Ontario government with respect to the further discussion of this Bill?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand my hon. friend's question to be whether the government has had any correspondence with the Ontario government. As far as I know, none whatever. I do not understand at this stage of the Bill what can be the object of my hon. friend's asking that it should be postponed. There has been a good deal of misapprehension regarding this Bill. I do not know how it has arisen.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

speechtext: This is the first time we have had a frank admission from any member of the government that the Bill of 1901 was actually a Bill to dam the St. Lawrence river. That throws new light on the matter to-night. That was denied the other evening by those who were supporting the Bill, but this amendment frankly admits that the Bill of 1901 gave authority to dam the St. Lawrence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Part of it, certainly.
The Canadian part of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Part of it.
The First Minister frankly admits that to-night and throws new light on the subject.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As I read that Act the power is given to dam the St. Lawrence for the purpose of generating energy, and whether it was wise or unwise to give that power, no action has been taken upon it. When we were asked to agree to plans for damming the St. Lawrence, the matter was referred to the Waterways Commission which has still the subject in hand. For my part I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes); I do not want to see the St. Lawrence dammed, and that is why, to meet the objection raised by some members on both sides of the House, the present amendment has been introduced which makes it clear that nothing under the present Bili can be done or shall be done so as to enhance or favour or forward what was done by the Act of 1901. And so, if this Bill is passed no injury can accrue to those who want to have the St. Lawrence remain as it is.

Did I understand the Prime Minister tq say that this company erected a dam under the Act of 1901?
Sir W'lLFRID LAURIER. I understand they did some work.
The Minister of Railways will bear witness to the fact that they never built any dam at all. The government built and paid for a dam from the mainland to Sheiks island.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That was long before the Bill of 1901.
Mr. M. P. Davis had the contract from the government for building that dam.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Possibly.

There is no question about it at all; I know the facts very well. That is really part of the canal system, and it is exactly the same as if a person leased power from the government on the Lachine canal or the Cornwall canal. Of course,

Mr. Davis had the advantage, when he was building the dam, of knowing that the power would be there, and so to-day he is paying a rental to the government, he having built his wheel pits within the government dam. But, the very fact that the Minister of Public Works started the other night that this Bill is really part of the proposal to dam the St. Lawrence-
The Minister of Public Works did not say that.
The Minister of Public Works stated that this Bill was really subsidiary to the other.

No such thing. I must correct my hon. friend. I made no such statement to this committee. I have been greatly misrepresented outside the House, and now my hon. friend is misrepresenting me inside the House. On the contrary, I stated that this Bill in my judgment had nothing to do with the question of damming the St. Lawrence. As to that, my mind was open; I had not formed a judgment one way or the other.
If my recollection is correct, the minister said that he had no doubt that this company proposed to get its power from the St. Lawrence Power Company.
If it should be developed.
I do not know that there was any qualifying phrase of that kind
I said that if that power were developed I suspected that this company would get its power there, but at the same time I had no knowledge on the subject.

At all events, my impression from what the minister said was that this Bill was to be considered in conjunction with the Bill that should come at a later date, so far as the damming of the St. Lawrence was concerned.
I made no such statement.
