speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must point out that when an hon. member denies having made any statement, his denial must be accepted irrespective of any other reference.

There is another thing I want to say to the Prime Minister. When this Bill was before the Private Bills Committee, we urged that this St. Lawrence Power Company's Bill be amended in clause 10. The claim was that the St. Lawrence Mr. J. D. REID.
Power Company could only go to a place called Hoople's creek, ten or twelve miles above Cornwall, for their power. If they had amended clause 10, there would not have been any objection to extend the scope of the St. Lawrence Power Company westward to Brockville or eastward to the Lachine canal. When the people interested in this Bill went to Prescott and Brockville they did not hesitate to say that this Bill had to go through, because the damming of the St. Lawrence was part and parcel of the whole affair, as they had not the power at Cornwall, all the power they had was sold, and they could not possibly supply the power from the St. Lawrence Power Company. But when they came back here they tell a different story. They say they have plenty of power at the St. Lawrence Power Company, and no doubt they have. The answer I gave to them at Prescott was that there was plenty of power there, and if the people of Brockville and Prescott would subscribe for plenty of power it would pay them to extend their transmission line to those places. If they refuse to give the people the advantage of a cheap power, we could ask the government to cancel the contract which they have for lighting the canal, amounting to $52,000 or something like that for 89 years, and there is no doubt that they would run their transmission line to Prescott and Brockville rather than have that contract cancelled. They would have no trouble in running their transmission line to Brockville or even to Kingston, as they say they are anxious to do. Mr. Beach, who has a water-power at Iroquois, has put in a new plant and is ready to serve the public. It is true, he has only put in machinery for 500 horsepower, but he has 2,000 horse-power that he is anxious to sell at Prescott and Brockville if it would pay to run a transmission line. In coming from Hoople's creek to Prescott, I understand that this St. Lawrence Power Company are going to buy the right of way for a width of 30 or 40 feet along the Grand Trunk railway. If they purchase that they will have no trouble in running their transmission line, and they do not need to have an extension of their charter for that purpose. Of course, if they were running on the public road, they would require to get a by-law from the municipality. Mr. Beach had no trouble in getting a by-law passed for that purpose. Down there the whole story was the damming of the St. Lawrence. Now they turn round and say that they are going to supply power from the St. Lawrence Power Company. That company, in the first place, would not agree at what price they would supply the power. They are supplying it to Cornwall for $12.50, and they are charging the government $63. There is no trouble about their getting to Prescott and

Brockville if they want to do that. So far *a:	Montreal is concerned, I think the
Prime Minister will admit that it is pretty well supplied with power. From the Beau-harnois canal there will be 75,000 horsepower, I have heard some engineers state that at the very least there will be 50,000 horse-power soon going from there to Montreal. Then, there is plenty of power from the Lachine canal, Shawenegan and Cedar rapids. In regard to this scheme for damming the St. Lawrence, let the Prime Minister just look at the situation. The proposed dam is to be right where the government territory commences to run eastward on both sides of the river. This government gave permission a few years ago to this same crowd, who are practically the Standard oil people, to dig a canal from the St. Lawrence to empty into the Grass river on the American side. The same people own the Massena power plant on the other side of the river, but they are rnly using a small portion of that power.
They have developed 35,000 horse-power now.

That canal empties into the Grass river, which empties again into the St. Lawrence. If this dam goes across the Long Sault, and they simply place a dam at the end of Grass river where there is thirty or forty feet of a rise, it is going to send the water down through the state, and they will have not only a water course, but they will have power-all the way down that state. From what people tell me it is worth an immense amount, and I am told that a canal system can be run from that point to Lake Champlain. If that is the case the Prime Minister will see that grain can be brought to that point, and carried down that way to Lake Champlain. Now the only reason they can urge for pushing this Bill through this session would be to get a supply of power for Prescott and Brockville. I am satisfied from what I have heard from good lawyers that they will have no trouble to buy the right of way, and carry that line up to Prescott and Brockville. If they can do that, I do not see any great rush for this Bill. Let it be held over, and let the government go into the matter, and bring it up at a future session.

If this Bill had anything to do with damming the St. Lawrence river I would hesitate very much before I would support it. Unlike some hon. gentlemen, I speak of the situation as having lived along it most of my life. It is not only on the map that I know it, but I have walked over the ground time and again. I am not going to discuss the question of damming the St. Lawrence river. That is a pretty big problem, and we will discuss
it at the proper time, if the time ever comes. But this Bill has nothing to do directly or indirectly with damming the St. Lawrence river, and cannot be construed as having any such purpose after the amendment proposed by the promoter of this Bill, and a discussion along those lines is calculated to lead us away from the purpose of the Bill.
May I ask the minister if the Bill had anything to do with damming the St. Lawrence before the amendment was introduced by the mover of the Bill?

I never understood that it had. I say frankly that I appeared before the Private Bills Committee, not as a member of the government, but as a member for the constituency affected, and very seriously affected, and all I suggested to the committee was that they give us a Bill for the incorporation of a transmission line, and nothing else. That is all I ever favoured, that is all I favour now, and that is all I believe there is in this Bill. It is all very well for hon. gentlemen who . are going to be supplied with cheap power in their own locality, to withhold sympathy from our attempt to get the power which we have not now.
Did the town of Brockville try to get this power, or was it presented to them?

For five .years the Brockville people have been discussing with Mr. Beach, and endeavouring to get together on terms to form a company to transmit power from Iroquois. It is with the sole desire to get power into a part of the country that has not any power, that I want this Bill put through, and any hon. gentleman in the House would do the same thing if lie were true to his own constituents. Now as to the damage to be done, nobody need tell me anything about damage to lie done if the St. Lawrence river is to be dammed. I have lived there, and know all about it, I know where the ice jams occur, and what is the result. But that has nothing to do with this Bill. This Bill has been shorn of everything that can lend suspicion that it is a back door attempt to dam the St. Lawrence river.
Would the minister tell us why these plans were all prepared in connection with a company?

Yes, certainly. These plans were prepared because a company has been trying to get permission to dam the St. Ilawrence for some years, and these are their propositions. They wanted to get the power, but the government has not given them the power. The Prime Minister stated a year ago that nothing 1 would be done without taking parliament
COMMON .a
into the full- confidence of the government. But I come back to this point. In so far as the town of Brockville is concerned, they have made many attempts to get power, and no serious effort has been made by any person outside Brockville to give us that power. True, some letters have been written intimating that such an attempt has been made, but I say that no serious attempt was ever made, and we are as far from getting power to-day as we ever were. That makes a very difficult situation for a town the size of Brockville. I may say that what is now one of the largest industries in the Dominion of Canada had its nucleus in the town of Brockville, a manufactory of agricultural implements. The stock of that company was purchased from local men, the local men understanding that the company was to be established in Brockville and would enlarge its business. But the question of power immediately came up and as we did not have the power we lost the industry, although we offered, I think, an unreasonable proposition in the way of a site and in the way of bonuses. The hon, member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) has pointed out the ground on which I wanted this Bill put through.
Did they ever apply to the Hydro-Electric Commission to get the power?

They did, they asked for bread and they got a stone, absolutely. Wliat I said a few moments ago, I mean emphatically, that no serious effort was made to give them any power from outside sources, and any person that makes any other statement says what is absolutely untrue, because I know all about it. I think there is some surplus power with a company now at Cornwall, the St. Lawrence Power Company. It must be remembered that this power is leased to them by the Dominion government in the manner outlined by the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid). I am of the opinion that they have surplus power that they can give to somebody. There is a power, or the nucleus of a power, generated opposite Mor-risburg, in the village of Waddington, a power I know very well, in what is known as the Little river, nearly opposite Mor-risburg, or a mile further west. The situation is something like that at the Sault. There is the main channel of the St. Lawrence river on the north, there is Ogden's Island, and to the south of that is the Little river. Years ago they had a dam across the Little river at Waddington and a paper mill there. That power has passed into the hands of another company. I am not sure but that if they had a transmission line, power could be obtained from that source. Then we come to Iroquois where Mr. Beach has some surplus power, but I am of the opinion it will never be of use Mr. GRAHAM.
until somebody builds a transmission line. Now without any thought of damming the St. Lawrence river to get power, I do. not see why this House should not grant a charter to a transmission line, a charter robbed of everything else, and give us an opportunity to get the power that runs along that- line for the development of our industries. That is all I have asked for, and all I want. And 1 do not think it is reasonable that the House, in the face of the present situation, with the Bill amended as I want it amended, so as to give the company no power except to run a transmission line-I say that I think it is not treating that part of the province fairly, it is not treating the constituency I represent fairly to say, when we think we have a chance to get power in this way that we should not have the right to have a transmission line for that power. I know the situation thoroughly, and I say again that all we are asking for and all that is wanted is power to transmit electricity. If it is not granted under such a Bill as this, we cannot get it. I believe there is power enough already developed along the route of that transmission line to supply the towns that are asking for power.

Does the hon. minister think that this is not in any way connected witn the St. Lawrence Power Company or that when this Bill is passed the one company will not be the complement of the -other? If not, why is this called The St. Lawrence Power Transmission Company,' while the other is ' The St. Lawrence Power Company'? I take it, the ownership is the same in both cases, and one company is the complement of the other, the one intended to develop power and the other to transmit it.

I did not see the BiL when it was first drawn, but as it stands now it precludes this transmission line from taking the power from works not already constructed. So, this transmission company is tied down to powers developed in -works now established and constructed. So, that gets over the objection of my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) altogether. And I think it -ought to.

I am sura the House was pleased with many of the remarks of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who leads it, and agrees with him to a great extent in those remarks. I did, for my part. He was opposed to a scheme to dam the St. Lawrence. He sympathized with those who were suspicious of the Bill before the House. But when these amendments were introduced bv the hon. gentleman who moved the Bill, all objection was Temoved from the right hon. gentleman's mind, because he saw at once that, by the very reason of this amend-

ment. the Bill, which up to that time, amply justified suspicion on both sides of the House, was robbed of any features that might justify suspicion. Possibly the right hon. gentleman may view the Bill from one standpoint and I from another. But I would ask hon. members to consider what this amendment is, and see if it justifies the conclusion that the right hon. gentleman-perhaps I might say a little too confiding in his opinion of the promoters of the Bill-has reached in connection with this matter. Let us read the amendment:
Nothing herein contained shall be deemed to constitute an approval by parliament of any future development of water-power by erecting a dam in or across the St. Lawrence river under the Act 1 Edward VII., chapter 3, intituled: ' An Act to incorporate the St. Lawrence Power Company,' or otherwise..
Suppose that the amendment had not been moved at all, how in the world would the Bill differ from what it is ? Can anybody suggest the slightest thing in which the Bill minus this amendment is different from the Bill plus this amendment? There is nothing in this Bill about damming the St. Lawrence. Nobody has ever contended that this Bill said anything that would give the right to anybody to dam the St. Lawrence. And, inasmuch as it does not give that right, how can it affect the existing condition to put in a clause declaring that nothing contained in the Bill shall be deemed to constitute an approval by parliament of that course?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Read the Balance, please.

One tiling at a time. There are two clauses. So far as the first clause is concerned, the law would be precisely the same without this amendment as it will be with it. Now, if we find a clause inserted which is obviously meaningless, yet so artfully drawn that it appealed to the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) himself-even though ft. may be, he has more confidence in the promoters of this Bill than some other members of the House have-and who, reading it cursorily, thought it meant something, is not that reason why we should be -all the more suspicious of the real purpose behind this Bill ? The amendment goes on:
Nor shall the company hereby incorporated he authorized to transmit power generated by the St. Lawrence Power Company other than the power generated by and in connection with the works already constructed by the said St. Lawrence Power Company.
That is to say, this company is asking the authority to transmit only the power which can be manufactured by the St, Lawrence Power Company with its development up to date Why does not the St,
Lawrence Power Company transmit its own electricity ? We have been told by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr Graham) that the object of the Bill is simply and solely to give this new corporation the power to transmit electricity. If the original company had not authority to transmit electricity, there must be some ground for that argument. But has the St. Lawrence Power Company the right to transmit electricity or has it not? There cannot he the shadow of a doubt about it. Section S says:
8.	The company may-
(a)	manufacture, use, supply and dispose of
electricity, water and gas, and water, hydraulic or other power by means of wires

There are your wires.
-cables, pipes, conduits, machinery or other appliances.
So, not only has it the power to manufacture electricity,-which would be an idle boon in itself -but it has the right to transmit it by any known means. And, that there may be no doubt that it is intended that they should have the power both to produce and transmit their powers are defined by restriction at one point, Section 9 says:
(b)	The company shall not permit any wire to be less than twenty-two feet above such highway or public place.
So, not only have they the express power to transmit electricity, but they are further circumscribed in the limitation of not being allowed to place any wire less than 22 feet above the public street. Thus, it is clear that the original power company had and has to-day, the right to erect its line and transmit all the power manufactured.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Not over the same territory that this Bill covers.
Practically the same territory.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
No.
Mr. NORTHRUP, What limit does the hon. member (Mr. Pardee) find in the original Act ?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Only as far as Hoople's creek.

I think the hon. member has been confused by a clause which does limit the power of the company, and which, perhaps, incidentally, sheds a light on this Bill. But that clause has nothing to do with the transmission of electricity. The other evening, I referred to the dif ference between the two Bills and I may take the liberty of doing it again. Section 14, of the St. Lawrence Power Company's Act gives the company power of expropriation, but limits it in this way:

Lands actually required for the construction and maintenance of the power canals, water-courses, raceways and reservoirs necessary for the utilization or operation of water-powers belonging to the company may be taken and acquired by the company.
And the Railway Act is applied thereto. But the lands referred to are simply those that the company may wish to expropriate for the construction of buildings and reservoirs in connection with their works. But we find that the present Bill proposes greater powers in regard to expropriation. And it may be that that is the secret of the present Bill. When we find that the power company has the right to do all that hon. members opposite, and the Minister of Railways, and the gentleman who promotes the Bill, say is asked by this Bill, is it any wonder that we on this side are doubly suspicious? When we consider the powers asked for by the new company, we find that they are powers generally to expropriate under the Railway Act. And one must not forget the case from British Columbia-the province vs. the Canadian Pacific railway, I believe it was-in which it was held that where, under the Railway Act, expropriation is made of lands which are vested in the Crown for the purposes of the province, that expropriation may lawfully be made. It is perfectly clear that under the original St. Lawrence Power Company Act they would have no power to expropriate the lands vested in the Crown for the benefit of the province for the transmission of electricity. They might do so for the construction of works and building of reservoirs, but it is clear that they would not have power beyond that limited purpose. In this Bill the land of the province whether under the bed of the river or wherever it may be, could be expropriated because the Railway Act applies generally giving the power of expropriation to this company just us to a railway company. When we find these suspicious circumstances the right hon. gentleman and those beside him might not be surprised if we said frankly with him that if we believed that this Bill was only to allow a certain amount of electricity generated to be transmitted, we would have no objection

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What else is there in the Bill?

I have been trying to point out several objectionable features and one is that the present St. Lawrence Power Company has the right to develop and transmit electricity. At the same time when we find a Bill of this kind coming in and being fought so vigorously for such a trifling purpose, that too is enough to make us suspicious, and if any one will read the history of the unfortunate negotiations which began by the contract between M.

P. Davis and the late administration, he will be confirmed in those suspicions. I have no desire to so far forget my duty as to relieve the late government from blame, because I think they are deserving of a great deal of blame for the bargain the Conservative party made with M. P. Davis. I think it was an improvident and improper bargain, and should not have been made, but it was made. If the right hon. gentleman takes up the history of that case from the time it was started with that improper bargain he will find that if liis predecessors chastised the people of this country with whips, he arid his government have chastised them with scorpions, because in 1900, when for the first time something was intended to be done, a new contract was made by the right hon. gentleman's administration, ten times worse than the original contract. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would have less confidence in the promoters of this Bill and their intentions if he bore in mind that the contract made in 1900 was an illegal contract. I would not venture to tell'the minister that they had made an illegal and improvident contract were it not that I had been fortified by a legal opinion which the right hon. gentleman would not dispute. The Auditor General refused to pay accounts, and he obtained the opinion of Mr. A. B. Aylesworth, K. C., of Toronto, before that hon. gentleman became a member of the government, as one of the leaders of the bar in Ontario. He informed his client, the Auditor General, frankly, freely and honestly, as of course he would always give his opinion, that it was an utterly illegal contract. When we find that the origin of this transaction was an illegality, and when we see the continuous difficulty experienced by the Auditor General year after year in trying to protect the treasury from the very gentlemen who are behind this Bill, I think we are justified in this year 1910 in saying that we are suspicious of another Bill, professing to attain so trifling an end, and employing so much material to obtain it. If we are wrong and hon. gentlemen opposite are right, then if the Bill were allowed to stand over for a year, could any grievous wrong be done to any one? The power has not been used. The public has got along without it. It is asserted that this is a part of a larger scheme and I am sure no member would defend the larger scheme if it is as it is represented to be. If that be the case and the worst that could happen by throwing out or postponing this Bill is that the people of the St. Lawrence will be further delayed in obtaining the electricity which they have not yet obtained, that will not be a very serious matter. But if we are right and the hon. gentlemen opposite are wrong, if, as many of us in the province of Ontario believe, the effect of this Bill is to

complete a contract intended to be made, and supposed to be made in 1900, but which by an oversight of the draughtsman was not made, surely it is better that this country should be protected, even now, than when it is too late we should discover what we have done. Hon. gentlemen must remember that it is a matter of common notoriety that Canada, owning great powers there, has derived little from them, and many of them are gone. One thousand dollars a year is all the Dominion receives from the dam which the Dominion built. It is a matter of common report that not more than $100,000 to $120,000 were expended by the St. Lawrence Power Company, and they sold out for nearly one million dollars. That means that parliament has already made a present to these fortunate individuals of nearly $1,000,000. Under these circumstances i appeal to the right lion, gentleman not to hurry the House into legislation which it might be impossible for us to retract. I venture to say to him that if the Bill of 1901 were being proposed to-day, it would not take us long to secure what we are asking, that it should at least stand over until the next year. I think we are all to blame for allowing that Bill to pass the House. Probably the right hon. gentleman did not know more about it than I did personally at that time; we all know how these Bills pass through the House.

mation. That seems to connect the two institutions. It seems to me that there is no doubt that by the Bill of 1901 power was given to the St. Lawrence Power Company to erect a dam upon the St. Lawrence river extending to the international line. In that case we have to consider whether or not we are going to supplement that Act by means of the Bill before the House today. I am quite safe in saying, I think, that had we the St. Lawrence Power Bill before us to-day we would not give our consent to it. The St. Lawrence Power Bill of 1901 gave the right to that company to generate and transmit electricity, and the reason for the present Bill, in my humble opinion, is that the Bill of 1901, while it gave power to generate and transmit electricity, did not give a power that this company 'are* getting, namely, the power to enter municipalities and take from private individuals their property without consent. These powers of expropriation are omitted from the Bill of 1901, and they simply want these powers to-day to supplement the powers which they got in 1901. I venture to say that the hon. gentleman who is promoting this Bill will not consent to the expunging of the expropriation powers. Otherwise the Bill is altogether useless to be used in conjunction with the Bill of 1901. That being the case, we must consider these two Bills together, and we must consider whether we are prepared to grant the company the rights contained in this Bill. The Bill gives them all the powers of expropriation contained ip. the Railway Act as far as they are applicable, and in addition it gives them further powers. It provides that the word ' land ' as used in the Railway Act, shall include the words ' easement or privilege '. In other words, the company have the right to purchase by expropriation, not only land as provided for in the Railway Act, but also easements and privileges. So that, in considering all the powers that they have we have to add the words ' easement and privilege ', to ' land ' as specified in the Railway Act. What would be the effect of this legislation? Take section 151 of the Railway Act, which is the expropriation clause and reading that section into this Act the language would be as follows. This company will have the power to:
Purchase, take and hold of from any person, any lands, easements or privileges, or other property necessary for the construction, maintenance and operation of its works and also alienate, sell or dispose of, any lands, easement, privilege or property of the company which for any reason have become not necessary for the purposes of this undertaking. .
Take section 176, read into that the provision of this Bill, and it will read as follows :

The company may take possession of, use or occupy any lands, easements or privileges belonging to any other transmission company, use and enjoy the whole or any portion thereof, &c.
Then take section 179. Where it says that lands may be taken without the consent of the owners, it will read ' lands, easements, or privileges ' and it will provide that these will be taken without the consent of the owners. Section 180 provides that the company shall file plans shewing the route of their proposed transmission line. That section will be quite applicable to the proposed company. Section 192 provides that:
The deposit of a plan, profile and book of references, and the notice of such deposit, shall be deemed a general notice to all parties o-f the lauds, easements and privileges which will be required for the purposes of the company.
I would like to know if that section is going to apply. It shows into what entanglements one may be led by making the Railway Act apply to a company organized for the transmission of electricity, and I am sure we would never consent to passing it in its present condition. It would give the right to this company to construct their poles over the houses and barns of private owners. Once you grant the right of expropriation they can expropriate that right so long as they compensate for the injury. As this Bill gives them the right to expropriate an easement or privilege they have the right to construct their wires along the sides, or on top of houses, or on the poles of other companies. I am sure it is not the intention of this parliament to allow this company any such pri-lege. Then, there is the right to expropriate private property which is expressly excepted from the Act of 1901. The Act of 1901 says that:
Nothing herein contained shall be deemed to authorize the company to enter upon any private property for tile purpose of erecting, maintaining or repairing any of its works, without the previous assent of the owner or occupant of the property for the time being.
This gives the company that privilege and it is for that very purpose, for the purpose of getting what they were not given in 1901 with "respect to the transmission of electricity, that this company are making application to-day. In addition, they have the right, without the consent of the municipality, to go to the municipality, and erect their transmission line. That right is expressly excepted from the Act of 1901 by section 9 which says:
The company for the purpose of constructing and maintaining its works may with the consent of the municipal council or other authority having jurisdiction over the same enter on any highway, square or other publio

place and as often as the company thinks proper, may with like consent op^n any highway, square or public place, &c.
There is no provision for compulsory expropriation under this Act. Taking all these facts into consideration, and speaking now upon the Bill itself-and there are many other objectionable matters that could be brought to the attention of the government if I were to speak in connection with the St. Lawrence Power Company and its proposed plans to be submitted to the government-but, simply speaking of the Bill itself as it appears before us it should not pass in its present shape. I claim that the amendment suggested by the promoter of the Bill does not in any wav safeguard the public; on the contrary I hold that it is injurious to the public. The first part of the amendment says:
Nothing herein contained shall be deemed to constitute an approval by parliament of any future development of water-power by erecting a dam in or across the St. Lawrence river under the Act 1 Edward VII., chapter 3, intituled: 'An Act to incorporate the St. Lawrence Power Company,' or otherwise.
That means nothing because if the company has the power now we are not taking it from it then, and if it has not the power we are not giving it, so that it makes no difference. The amendment goes on to say:
Nor shall the company hereby incorporated be authorized to transmit power generated by the St. Lawrence Power Company other than the power generated by and in connection with the works already constructed by the said St. Lawrence Power Company.
This means that we prohibit the St. Lawrence Power Company from passing over its transmission line any power except such as is at present generated, by works already constructed and what the petition presented to the House states is 2,300 horse-power, and as that petition also states they are capable of developing 6,000 horse-power we are in fact restricting them from transmitting about 4,000 horse-power over these proposed lines. In other words we are actually preventing the development of the resources of the power already there to be used in this country, and we. are practically providing a means by which the power shall go somewhere else, probably across into the United States. Now, I would like to know whether this parliament is going to have an opportunity of assenting to or rejecting the proposed plans of the St. Lawrence Power Company. The Minister of Public Works seems in some of his remarks to indicate that parliament is not going to be consulted. On the 13th of March, 'Hansard' page 5507 he said:
Such information has not come to me and I am not aware of it having come to any
other member of the government, or any other department. With regard to the compensation to be paid, I, as Minister of Public VVorks, have been called on to consider the matter with the view of determining what would he fair to Canada in ease we should finally approve of these works; and I am prepared to say that, so far as my department is concerned-and it will have a goo*i deal to do with the fixing of rates-it will recommend to council that no agreement he entered into and no approval, be given the works of the company unless there goes into the treasury of Canada as much revenue from this power as will go into the treasury of the state of New York.
From this it would seem quite plain that the Minister of Public Works does not think it is necessary to come to parliament to say what compensation shall be paid by this company for the power they propose to get. It seems to me that under the provisions of the Act of 1901 it may not be necessary for the company to come here, because we have already passed legislation saying they may build a dam to the centre of the River St. Lawrence to the international line, and on the other side the state of New York has given the Long Sault Company similar power, so that when they have their works constructed in each respective case they will have a complete dam across the St. Lawrence river, and then all they need have is the approval of the Governor in Council as mentioned in the Act of 1901. I would like to have an assurance from the Prime Minister that the government shall not in this case act by order in council, but that this parliament will have something to say as to what they shall pay for that power just as the legislature of the state of New York had the right to fix the compensation to be paid on the other side. I wish an assurance upon this point?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Upon what point?
Upon the question whether or not under the Act of 1901 the fixing of remuneration to be paid will be by order in council or by a Bill submitted to this parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think I remember that I stated lauo year that in a matter of this kind the government would not take any action except after consulting parliament.	.
Would the Prime Minister be willing to have a clause to that effect inserted in this Bill?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would not have any objection at all.

It does not seem to me that the government can be quite as 1 indifferent to a Bill of this kind as the

Prime Minister suggests. The modern doctrine in Great Britain at least is that the government by virtue of their control of parliament are held responsible not only for public legislation, but for private legislation as well. It seems to me that much the same rule ought to prevail here. But even assuming that such would not be the case in ordinary instances we must remember that this is not an ordinary case This is a proposal to deal with a great international water-way. It is a proposal also to enter into a scheme which may affect at some time or other international relations, and. therefore, it is of the utmost possible importance that the Bill, although introduced as a Private Bill, should nevertheless be most carefully considered by the administration, and that the government should have absolute responsibility with regard to it. I do not see how the government can avoid that responsibility. I understand it is not a government measure in the ordinary sense, but still in respect to a subject of this kind it seems to me the government must accept responsibility as direct, and as immediate as if this Bill were a government measure. Now, the Act of 1901 was passed without any discussion whatever in this House. There was no discussion on the second reading or on the third reading or in the committee. I was in the House at that time, and in common with my hon. friend from Hastings I have to accept the responsibility for the fact that there was no discussion. But one reason for that I suppose was that a great many of these Bills which do not attract attention are accepted in Committee of the Whole House by reason of the fact that they have been passed by the Select Committee. I do not suppose that any member of this House at that time grasped the full significance of the language which is to be found in section 8 of that Bill. That section conferred upon the St. Lawrence Power Company, which as we all know, and as has been practically admitted, is only another name for the company which is promoting this Bill. I do not think it * has been denied that the persons who control the St. Lawrence Power Company are the promoters of this Bill.

Pardon me a moment- the two companies are owned, and controlled by the Long Sault Construction Company. The St. Lawrence Power Company, and the St. Lawrence Transmission Company are owned, and controlled by the Long Sault Company, and I challenge denial of that statement.	.

The St. Lawrence Power Company under another name is now coming to parliament for some further rights and privileges. It is not important at the present moment to consider how far-Mr. K. L. BOEDEN.
reaching the powers it wants from parliament may be. It wants those powers for the purpose of carrying out a scheme. That scheme involves the damming of the St. Lawrence. They have power at the present time* under one of their charters, to dam the St. Lawrence as far as the international boundary. That has not been and cannot in my opinion be successfully denied. There is a certain qualification upon the power thus conferred upon them. That qualification is contained in the proviso to be found in subsection (a) of clause 8 of the Act of 1901. It is in these words:
Provider! that the works hereby authorized shall not be commenced until the plans thereof have first been submitted to and approved by the Governor in Council.
My right hon. friend said on a previous occasion, I think it was last session, or it may have been this session, that he regarded that project as of such vital importance to the people of this country that nothing would be done to carry it out without the consent of parliament. That, I understand, to be his position; if it is not, he will correct me. I would suggest to him that, if that be his position, it would be proper now to say to this- company, which is coming here under another name; ' The importance of the rights which were conferred upon you in 1901 was not recognized at the time; it is more fully recognized now, for many reasons which I need not stop to enumerate. For one thing, we realize, more than we did in 1901, the very great importance to the people of these water-powers.' Why, then, would it not be opportune, when this company is asking for further privileges, to insert in this Bill a distinct provision making it absolutely necessary that the approval of parliament shall be obtained before any such plans are approved? The right they have obtained is a qualified right; it is subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. Would it not be a fair and reasonable proposition, in view of what has since transpired, and in view of the importance of this subject in the eyes of the people of this country, that we should go a step further and say that the Governor in Council shall not approve of any plans until those plans have been first submitted to and approved by parliament. I would suggest that to the right hon. gentleman as a reasonable rider to this Bill, and it seems to me that it would go very far in the direction of satisfying certain criticisms which have been made on the Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have already stated to my hon. friend that for my part I have no objection at all, and I think
the government have no objection to such a proposition, because practically we

have stated that, whether we are bound by law or not, it is our intention to do so. Many people in this country are nervous in regard to the possible damming of the St. Lawrence. I have stated to the House the various objections, and for my part I have one also. At the present time, with the information I have, I would not consent on any consideration to have the St. Lawrence dammed. I give my opinion as to that with perfect candour. I may say to my hon. friend that I do not altogether admit the position he has taken, that I am responsible for all private legislation. There is private legislation of different kinds. For instance, there are divorce Bills fori which I cannot be held to be personally responsible. But the question of this Bill depends altogether on what powers are intended to be conferred b,y it. At first blush it is simply a Bill for the transmission of electrical energy. To the ordinary mind there is nothing objectionable at all in that. But the objection arises at the point that this electrical energy, must be generated somewhere, and the suspicion is that it would be generated by damming the St._ Lawrence. My hon. friends on the other side object to that. I am opposed to it also, and in ordeT to make the matter, perfectly plain I have no objection to accepting the amendment suggested bv the hon. leader of the opposition, that no works shall be carried on without the consent of parliament having been first obtained.

I may say that I hold my hon. friend politically though not personally responsible for all the divorces which have been granted in parliament, 1 have drawn up an amendment as I would suggest, although I cannot say that it has been very carefully considered. I will send a copy of it over to the right hon. gentleman, and perhaps he will look over it and in the meantime defer the consideration of the Bill.
Before the amendment is put, I wish to say that on the 14th of March, when this Bill was under discussion, I made the following statement:
REID Has your department power to do that without the consent of parliament?

I think not. Parliament will have to consent to the matter in the end. and my recollection is that some time a^o, in answer to a question put by the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) the Prime Minister stated that before the plans were approved of. the whole matter would be submitted to parliament for consideration, and before definite action would be taken, parliament must be satisfied that the work will he in the interest of Canada.
All the remarks I made as to what m,y department would do, as to requiring that at least one-half the power should be reserved for Canada, and as to the rates to 199
be charged for that power, were based upon the contingency as to whether or not the plans would be finally approved of, and I stated positively, not once merely, but twice, that the Prime Minister had given to parliament the assurance that the plans would not be approved of and that no action would be finaly taken until after th* whole matter had been submitted to parliament and parliament was satisfied that the work would be in the interest of Canada .

When the first application was made, I understand that the government's! engineers reported against1" it, but when it was considered a second time, the same engineers recommended it. Did not that look as if the government intended to approve of the project?

Not at all. That did not look to the action that the government or parliament might take. The charge has been made in some of the newspapers which have, i regret to say, twisted and distorted and falsified to a most extraordinary degree what took place during the very interesting and pleasant debate which lasted all night some time ago, that I had made the remark in the House that plans had been prepared some time ago; and one paper stated that those plans had been prepared by my department, and that I was not willing to make them public, and refused to produce them or to give an,y information in regard to them, conveying the impression that they had been kept secret. As early as the 14th of January, in answer to a question which had been put to me, I stated that the company had submitted plans of which they had asked the approval of the Governor in Council. I stated that the government had referred those plans to the engineers of the three departments of Public Works, Railways and Canals and Marine and Fisheries, and that the engineers had reported adversely to the plans; that subsequently, about a year afterwards, I think, new plans were presented, and those also were referred to the engineers,and they had reported rather favourably on them, with certain limitations; and'further that those plans had been referred to the International Waterways Commission. At the time when I was asked to produce the plans they were not in my possession, they were not in the po-ssession of my department, hut they were in the possession of a member of the International Waterways Commission. It was about midnight when I was asked to produce them. I stated that before the -Bill was finally disposed of, I would be happy to produce them, and that if the committee desired to have them I would produce them, even though the Bill had nothing whatever to do with the damming of the St. Lawrence.

I understood that the hon. gentleman was also asked to produce the report of the Waterways Commission and the Conservation Commission, because we were given to understand that one or both of these bodies had considered the question and reported. But I * have not been able to find that report.

The report which was asked for by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) was the report of the engineers. I stated that the commissioners had not yet reported. It has also been put forward in the press that the Act of 1901 had been concealed, and that the hon. member for Westmorland produced startling information to the House when he read that Act of 1901. The hon. member for Westmorland will do me the justice to say that it was I who called his attention to that Act, and it was sent for and he then read it to the House. I mention this in order to show that so far as I w as concerned, and the same remark will apply to every other member who was supporting this Bill, there was no disposition to keep back anything from the committee, no desire to withhold any information, Now, having made this statement, I desire to say that so far as I am concerned, I see no objection whatever to accepting the amendment proposed by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. My hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) said that if this was a transmission line pure and simple, and he could be satisfied of that fact, he would support the Bill Now, I would invite that hon. gentleman to suggest any statement, if by racking his brain he can think of any amendment which will make this more simply and more purely a transmission power Bill than it is, I for one would gladly accept it. I do not believe that language can be used to make it more clearly and purely a trans mission Bill, I do not think any other language can be used which would more surely prevent it from being a Bill for the generation of electrical energy or for the construction of any works for generating electricity; it is purely and simply a power transmission Bill. But if any amendment would make it so more clearly than the language which is used, I would support such an amendment. But, perhaps, that may not now be necessary in view of the amendment of the leader of the opposition, to which I have no objection.

Let me call the attention of the Minister of Railways to the fact that the chairman of the Hydro-Electric Commission, in the strongest terms has protested against this measure. At the same time he has presented facts to show that the town of Brockville and the district about it has been thoroughly investigated, engineers have gone over that road twice, Mr. iPUGSLEY.
and are prepared to furnish these municipalities with power in the near future. He distinctly says that the municipalities in eastern Ontario have applied for power to the Hydro-Electric-Commission, as appears by the following list:
Municipalities in easterji Ontario who have applied for power to the Hydro-Rlectrio Power Commission.	. .	[DOT]
Amount asked for by the municipality.
Kingston, 2,500 H.P.; Belleville, 3,200 H.P.; Deseronto, 300 H.P.; Brockville, 500 to 1,000 H.P.; Oshawa, 500 H.P.; Cobourg, 900 H P.; Bowmanville, 600 H.P.; Port Hope, Whitby and Picton. 500 H.P., no price quoted yet; Durham, 2,000 H.P., uo price quoted yet. Prescott and Napanee asked to be quoted on power, but no specific amount.
The minister must recognize this fact as well, that the Hydro-Electric Power Commission had the second and fourth reports of water-power prepared, and the territory covered by these reports lies between Toronto and Brockville.

My hon. friend asked me a question a moment ago. which I did not answer, because. I was called out. I know the complete history of the negotiations with Brockville. I repeat that so far as Brockville is concerned, there never was any serious attempt by the Hydro-Electric Commission to give them one ounce of power. Some letters were written, from which no result came. I think if my hon. friend will investigate, he will find that by the action of the legislature, no provision was made during last session for any power in this part of Ontario, but for the west. However, I repeat the assertion, that no serious attempt was ever made by the chairman of the Hydro-Electric Commission to give Brockville power, though one or two letters were written.

I do not know what the hon. gentleman means by serious attempt. The hon. gentleman knows that the fourth report was published in 1907, and in that report it is definitely stated, under the heading: 'Power conditions, in the St. Lawrence river district,' that Brockville with a population of 9,000 used an average horse-power of 900; Cornwall with a population of 7,600, used 4,485 horse-power; Iroquois, with a population of 1,200, used 85 horse-power; Gana-noque, with a population of 4,000, used 900 horse-power, and so on. I have a letter from the chairman of the Hydro-Electric Commission stating in the most emphatic language, that it is their purpose, just as early as possible, to establish the power transmission lines asked for, and have the people and municipalities in that district supplied with electric energy. He says in a letter to me:
We expect to continue the Niagara fine east probably as far as Brockville or even Prescott

and Cornwall, supplying the power from the Niagara in as far as economical, probably to Port Hope or Cobourg, the supply to be augmented at the Trent river, unless all the power of the Trent is absorbed by private companies in the meantime, and from some point farther east. Eventually we would have a continuous high voltage transmission system from Windsor in the west to Cornwall in tlje east.
we had little difficulty in getting power at a low price at Niagara Falls, viz., $9, as the province controls the developments there, but we will be helpless in the east if the development companies and transmission companies are operating under Dominion charters.
Now that is a most emphatic statement, and the minister knows full well that if these companies get Dominion charters, it will be practically impossible for the Hydro-Electric Commission to obtain that power from the St. Lawrence or from other water-powers.
One member suggested that the company should be compelled to sell power in Canada at the same price as they intend selling over in the United States. There is such a clause in the agreements with the companies at the Falls, and if we had not the drastic power that we have to expropriate, &c., we would not be buying power at $9, as the companies on the American side have an arrangement amongst themselves not to sell power for less than $18.
The minister knows full well that in the Ottawa district, where the Hydro-Electric Commission have control of the powers, they have had a profit of over $23,000 on the right side of the ledger, after deducting the charges of building the transmission lines here. As to the cost of power, I might read a little further from this letter:
There are three things that go to make up the cost of power; power at $9 at the Falls, interest on sinking fund and investment and operation. The price of power is fixed at $9, and all contracts have been let for the building of the line, and the fact that the cost is under the estimates enables me to say definitely that power will be delivered at the estimated cost price.
Yet the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) rose in his place the other evening, and told us that the powey would cost the municipalities of Ontario two or three times this amount.
It will be safer to multiply it by four.

We can easily put the hon. member's (Mr. Carvell's) knowledge of water-powers and transmission lines in a district about which he knows nothing in contrast with that of the man who is at the head of the Hydro-Electric Commission and knows all about it. Mr. Beck says;
The line is capable of transmitting 65,000 horse-power, the contracts amount to less than 199J
half this amount, and so you will readily see how the price will drop as the consumption increases. The city of Toronto offers power for ten hours, I understand, at $17.85 per horse-power.
One of the most serious matters in connection with the St. Lawrence power development, and the building of a dam in this country is the fact that Canada practically loses control of the St. Lawrence river as a navigable stream. The channel is diverted to the American side where locks are to be built, but not on the Canadian side.
The Minister of Railways and Canals referred to the maps that are before us. It was my privilege to investigate some of the other maps which I do not see here to-night, and which were in charge of the clerk. On one of these maps I noticed it was indicated that there would be on the American side of the boundary line 50 turbines., while on the Canadian side there would be only 11 turbines. And, taking into consideration the fact that the people of Canada can have no control over the laws of the state of New York, it would be absurd for us to expect that we should be able to compel an American company to transmit a portion of that power to Canada for the development of our industries. Let me read further from this letter:
The territory covered by these reports lies between Toronto and Brockville. Eleven municipalities in the territory have asked for estimates and negotiated with the commission for a supply of power, and others are about to apply.
If the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) was not aware of this fact, it is time he should be.
The object of the Hydro-Electric Power Commission is to supply power at cost to as many municipalities as possible, and the commission propose to provide a supply of power for all municipalities that can be advantageously served.
If the Bill is passed, the company would have authority to transmit power into a large section of the territory to be supplied by the commission, and a dual system of transmission lines would be the result. The commission has always considered that where municipalities are prepared to co-operate and so increase the demand for power from one source a dual system is a hindrance to municipalities in the working out of their plane, and such a system should not be encouraged.
*
After these emphatic statements by the chairman of the Hydro-Electric Commission of Ontario, directly opposed to this measure, after the statement of the chairman of the International Waterways Commission, of the Board of Trade of Montreal, of the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, of the provincial government of Ontario, and of practically all the navigation companies whose vessels ply on this
6256

river St. Lawrence, I cannot but feel that we are taking a step in the wrong direction in allowing this measure to pass at the present time. I sincerely hope it will be left over for another session to make a thorough investigation and see if it is not possible to have the provincial government of Ontario in control of this water-power.

Perhaps I shall bt pardoned if I participate a little in this-post mortem examination with respect to this Bill. I think it will be in the memory of every member of this committee that when this Bill was first committed to this Committee of the Whole the objection raised to it was largely upon the ground of it being an infringement of provincial rights and an interference with the HydroElectric .Commission of Ontario. Up to that point, I had not offered any suggestions to the committee with respect to the Bill. But, some information being in my possession at the time, I thought it was due to the committee that I should call the attention of hon. members to what I conceived to be a very much stronger objection to the acceptance of this Bill. I believed that this Bill (No. 115) was but a preliminary to another Bill that was to be introduced in parliament at this very session giving certain powers in connection with the damming of the River St. Lawrence. And, conceiving such a proposition to be against the best interests of Canada. I felt that- the time had come to raise objection. My hon friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr Pugsley) is quite correct in stating that he called my attention to the fact that it would not be necessary for any company to come to parliament to seek the power to dam the St. Lawrence, because that power was already granted them by Act of this parliament passed some years ago, a fact with which he was familiar, because there had recently come before him certain plans for approval, plans which could only come before him under authority of some Act, and under that Act the approval of the government was sought for these plans. 1 then, as I conceived it to be my duty, called the attention of the committee to the fact that this, after all, was a grand scheme to secure, in the interest of foreign capitalists, the water-powers that properly belonged to Canada. I think I mentioned on that- occasion that by reason of the darn that would necessarily be constructed, ninety per cent of the flow of water would be tb'-	tb- AmerK-M'i side. My hon.
friend the Minister of Public Works very properly said that that would be safeguarded, that there would be restrictions as to the use of this power, and that care would be taken that Canada's interests should be safeguarded and that at least half the power would be secured for Canadian industries. Well, it is one thing to Mr. ARMSTRONG.
make such a proposition, and it is another thing to carry it out; 1 think I said that, while you might have an arrangement, agreements and contracts, still it would be a matter of practical impossibility to enforce them. I objected to this Bill on the ground that it was part of a scheme to dam the St. Lawrence and secure for a great American corporation the water privileges of the St. Lawrence. I was not in full possession of the facts, but I said it was worthy of the consideration of this committee and of the House and of the people of Canada, and that we should wait in order that we might inquire and learn the facts. I have felt that much good was done by reason of the action which was taken in connection with this particular Bill, and I am the more convinced of it from what has transpired here to-night. The promoter of the Bill has proposed a -certain amendment, and there are certain other amendments which have been suggested, all of which I hope will be adopted. If any or all of these amendments -are adopted,, I think the House and the country can recognize that the sting has been taken out of the mouth and the rattle out of the tail of the rattle snake, and it does not now have even the semblance of a rattle snake. I have not been convinced of the necessity of a transmission-of-power line. I view the matter from this standpoint that with the power that has been developed there, with the power available for distribution, the company which developed that power has authority to transmit and to distribute, and I do not see the necessity of any new company being empowered by this parliament to distribute that power. The very first thing that convinced me that this was a part of a great scheme was the reading of part of section 6 where it says:
Lay and maintain pipes, cables, wires or other conductors and connect them with similar lines in other provinces and with simi- , lar lines in the United States for the purpose of importation only.
If this was a mere little innocent transmission power company to distribute the power being developed on the Canadian side, I cannot conceive of their coming to this parliament and asking for power to connect with lines in- the United States, and it is because of the wording of the Bill that I was led to -conclude that this Bill was part of a greater scheme and one that would be to the injury of Canada. I am confirmed in the belief that it was such a scheme,- but having in every way divested it of its power to do harm I am perfectly satisfied. The objection taken by me on a former occasion has, I think, been sustained and acknowledged and removed as far as it is possible to remedy legislation in that direction if you pass the Bill at all. The Minister of Railways has very fairly

made a plea in the interests of his constituency that some company shall be empowered to transmit the power that is already being developed. That is a question of fact as to the conditions prevailing. I am not in a position to judge of that; those representing St. Lawrence constituencies must be the best judges, and as the matter now stands I would feel free to support a harmless power transmission company. But I would not feel free to support any measure that would involve this country in conditions which prevail in some other sections of Canada to-day, by reason of the legislation of this parliament, as for example the conditions that are cropping up at Port Frances. These things we must guard against and I think we have guarded against them in this particular case. As the matter now stands, I feel at liberty with the amendments which have been suggested to support the Bill.

One reason why I submit the Bill should not go through is that it is admitted that the gentlemen who are in this company are to purchase the power from the St. Lawrence Power Company and then they will sell it to the towns of Prescott and Brockville, the Railway Commission having the right to fix the rates at which the transmission company sell to these towns. But the commission cannot regulate the rates at which it shall be sold by the power company to the transmission company and the transmission company have a capital of $200,000. The line will not cost $25,000 and they will make the people pay a dividend on a lot of watered stock and a double profit. If the Minister of Railways and Canals is so anxious, as I believe he is, to get power to Brockville, it has been argued here that the St. Lawrence Power Company now have power to run a transmission line to Brockville. If he will say to this company; Run your transmission line to Brockville at once or otherwise I will cancel your contract, that line would be built. We are paying $52,000 a year to that company for 400 horse-power to open and shut the gates and are not using more than 45 horse-power. We pay $63 a horsepower, and when the government confirmed that contract in October, 1900, just before the elections, the company were selling power at Cornwall at $12.50 a horse-power. That contract for 400 horse-power is for 89 years. The present Minister of Justice, on the application of the Auditor General, gave an opinion saying possibly the making of this contract was a distinct infraction of section 11 of the Act respecting the Department of Railways and Canals, Revised Statutes of Canada, ch. 37, which says:
The minister shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of all works except in cases of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to tbe public interest or in which the nature of the work 't can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the minister.
The contract they have is illegal, and it was in 1900 that this government amended the old contract. The late minister, Mr. Blair, amended and extended it. If the Minister of Railways thinks that this Bill would do that then where we would have the advantage of getting cheaper power would be that the Railway Commission would deal with the St. Lawrence Power Company. Supposing this transmission company that is being formed, say: We have to pay the St. Lawrence Power Company $20 or $25 per horse-power, and we are only asking $2 to $3 per horse-power more; nobody could object to that. I cannot see where we are going to get any benefit from the clause in this Bill which says that the Railway Commission shall be referred to. Now, it has been admitted that this power is to come from the St. Lawrence Power Company. The men who are the incorporators of this transmission line company went to the Waterways Commission in Toronto and told them that they were getting this Bill passed, that they proposed to dam the St. Lawrence and they claimed that the damming of the St. Lawrence should be carried out in order that they might get this power. I appeal, in the interests of Brockville and Prescott, to the Minister of Railways, to make the St. Lawrence Power Company send that power up there. Then we will not have to deal with any middle company that we have no control over, and we can then insist that they shall give us a reasonable rate. I do not think that under the Railway Act we can get cheap power from the Railway Commission, but if they were not giving us a reasonable rate we could come to parliament and ask that the Bill be amended, so as to provide that the Board of Railway Commissioners could regulate the rate.
Under the Act of 1901, relating to the St. Lawrence Power Company, have they to submit their charges for power to the Railway Commission, or to anybody?

To no one at all. That is the point I raise. How are we going to get cheaper power under this transmission Bill? The St. Lawrence Power Company will say to those in this new company: We will put the price at $25 or $30 per horse-power, or whatever we like, and the only redress we have, if they are charging too much, is to ask the Railway Commissioners to regulate the price between this company and the other.

Under this Act this company would have to submit their rates

for transmission to the Railway Commission, would they not?

This company will, but it is the first company that is the main one, and that is the lame feature of this Bill. If there was the slightest doubt about the association of this company with the St. Lawrence Power Company, which I do not think there is, there might be some reason for it. I submit that this matter is so important that it should be laid over to give us a chance to get these things right, and not try to push it through in this way.

When I opposed this Bill before I did so because I could not understand why the St. Lawrence Power Company should come to parliament now and get a transmission line. There were very good grounds for being suspicious of the Bill because of the way in which it was introduced. The Bill certainly has been shorn of some of the powers that they asked for when they came before this House. But, I am not at all clear in my own mind up to the present whether there is not still, if J may use the expression, a nigger in the fence. The amendment proposed by the gentleman who promotes this Bill (Mr. Pardee), the statement made by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the amendment proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) go a long way towards cutting out anything that may be wrong in the Bill, but at the same time what puzzles me is why, with the powers that they have under the Bill of 1901, if it is only a transmission line they want, they come before the House to-day with this Bill even in its present shape. The only point I can see wherein this Bill gives them some advantage that they do not possess under the old Bill is with respect do the right to acquire electrical energy. It seems to me that their object could be accomplished by amending the Bill of 1901 to enable them not only to generate electricity, but to acquire it from other private power companies existing in different parts of the country. They have thg right to transmit under their original Bill. I think, Mr. Chairman, that it has been a good thing that all this opposition has been raised. I think it was a first rate thing that we had an all-night session over this Bill. It has done one thing. It has aroused the people of Canada to the importance of the legislation that was passed by this House in 1901. I did not happen to be a member at that time. If I had been a member I would not have known any more of what that Bill meant than most of those who were in the House at that time.
Mr. PU6SLEY. Was it passed late at night?

No, but the Bill was like a great many Bills that go through this House almost every day; the average member of the House knows mighty little about . the real meaning of them. Had the members of this House, and the people of Canada realized what was being done by the Act of 1901 there would have been a howl from one end of the Dominion to the other. But, fortunately for us that Act is not all sufficient. Fortunately for the people of Canada, and this House the owners of that franchise have to come back and get their plans approved by the Minister of Public Works before they can go on and dani the River St. Lawrence. That has been our safeguard. I think that the thorough discussion-I will not say thorough discussion, because I do not know yet whether it has been thorough or not-but the long discussion that we have had over the matter has awakened us to what might easily and innocently have been done by any minister of the Crown in approving plans without realizing exactly what they mean. The waterpower at the Long Sault dam is a heritage for the people of Canada. It is not our heritage at the present moment, but it may be a heritage for our children, our grandchildren, and our great grandchildren. We do not want that power at the present time in Canada. For every horse-power that can be used within a reasonable distance of the Long Sault rapids there are to-day fifty horse-power that can be developed without going to the St. Lawrence river, which is an international stream.
Another thing we want to be very careful about is accepting engineers' Teports. Take the case of the water-power at Fort Frances, the facts regarding which have been made public. In that case the engineer was a man named Fanning, of whom I have heard for the last 15 years as the very first authority on hydraulic engineering in America. When Mackenzie and Mann established their large electrical power 60 or 70 miles east of Winnipeg on the Winnipeg river, they got this man to report to them before they took action. Now, what did Mr. Fanning do in this case? The promoter of the company, Mr. Backus, and the president of the company, went to the Ontario government with a report from this engineer that only 9,000 horse-power could 'be developed at Fort Frances, and they got the government to agree to the scheme on condition that 4,000 horse-power should be delivered on the Canadian side and the balance on the American side. But within a few months that same engineer gave a report that from 36,000 to 38,000 horse-power could be developed at Fort Frances, and the result was that 4,000 horse-power was to be used at Fort Frances and the balance of 34,000 horse-power on the American side. That shows how care-

ful we ought to be about engineers' reports before giving away franchises which we have no right to give away. I was delighted to hear the words of the Prime Minister to-night, and I agree with him that we should not at the present time give oyer this St. Lawrence power to a Canadian company, let alone to an American company, at any price they might pay to the state of New York for that privilege of damming the St. Lawrence on the American side. I can tell you, Sir, that their object is not, as they have stated to this House, to build up towns on the American and Canadian side of the rapids in the St. Lawrence. I happen to know that four or five months ago engineers came from New York to Ottawa to see what arrangements could be made for the securing of power in this vicinity, because they were not absolutely certain whether this thing would go through or not, and these engineers made the statement that the power could be transmitted from the Long Sault to the state of New York commercially. When you remember that from 600,000 to 800,000 horse-power can be developed there, look at what it would mean to them if they could export that, power to New York city. Does any one believe for a moment that if that dam were built and if from 300,000 to 600,000 horse-power were developed now, and we could not use it (as we could not at the present time) that that power would not be sent to the United States. And does any one believe for a moment that if that power were sent into the United States we would ever get it back. At Niagara, in proportion to the water on each side of the boundary, the Americans get double as much power as they are entitled to. For ten years the town of Fort Frances has been engaged in lawsuits with this American company which owns the franchise. One of the chief promoters of the St. Lawrence power stated in the city of Montreal that they had to have it and they were going to have it, and that when the power was developed they would give the Canadians 90 days in which to take the power, and if they did not take it then it would be sold in the United States. Well, I think he spoke a little too soon; I believe the people of Canada realize or are beginning to realize something of the value of that power and of their rights in the matter, and that they will not think of allowing any company, Canadian or American, more especially a foreign company, to dam the St. Lawrence right at the point where it becomes a Canadian river altogether. The St. Lawrence is one of the greatest rivers on the earth; it is a canal extending 1,000 miles right into the heart of the country, and if we allow that river to be dammed we do not know what we may be doing to impede navigation. One of the
best engineers in Canada told me that no man could tell at the present time what the effect of such a dam would be. He told me that some 50 years ago there was a small dam 12 feet high on the Mississippi near Almonte, and an ice jam raised the water 40 feet, with the result that the dam went out and every dam and every mill between that and the Ottawa river was swept away. If the same thing should occur on the river St. Lawrence the result might be appalling. But leaving all that aside it is too big a matter to allow any American company to control. I am no believer in government ownership in most cases, but this is a case where we have an international river where complications are apt to arise, and if the time ever comes- the time has not come yet and it will not come for a good while-when the waterpower on that river should be developed in the interests of Canada it ought to be a matter for the Dominion and American governments to engage in themselves and not transfer the doing of it to any company of American speculators. There has been a great deal of time spent in discussing this Bill, but the time has been well spent, and not a minute of it has been wasted. I think now that the government will realize how inadvisable it would be for them in the near future to approve of plans for damming the St. Lawrence. After what I have heard in discussing this matter with prominent men, I believe that no government would last a month that would allow the great St. Lawrence river to be dammed and controlled by an American company of speculators.

I have to congratulate the government, on its splendid attendance to-night. The Minister of Customs is absent, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is unfortunately absent, but every other Minister of the Crown is in his place to-night, I presume in the interest of this Bill. This shows the result of the opposition which was engendered against this Bill in the Private Bills Committee led by the members from Grenville and Dundas, and the member for North Ontario.
